subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and duty to present a petition from Canadians who reside in Toronto, Scarborough, Mississauga, Richmond Hill, and a few other places. They exercise their ancient and undoubted right to present a grievance.
They say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised, in the course of bilateral trade negotiations, that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised and that the proposed trade agreement denies Canadians secure access to the U.S. market which was the key objective in these negotiations.
Therefore, the undersigned, your petitioners, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

June 27, 1988
Petitions

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF RIGHTS OF THE UNBORN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two petitions to present to the House. The first is from the Pentecostal Assemblies of Canada and contains signatures from residents of Havelock, Norwood, and Peterborough. It deals with the issue of abortion.
The petition calls upon Parliament to pass into law legislation which will protect the life of the unborn child from conception through all stages of development, with the exception of the extremely rare situation in which an abortion is performed in order to save the life of the mother.

subsubtopic: RESEARCH INTO PREVENTION AND CURE OF SCHIZOPHRENIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a second petition from the Peterborough Chapter of the Friends of Schizophrenics. It contains over 500 signatures and deals with research into schizophrenia.
The petition calls on Parliament to ensure that research efforts related to schizophrenia will in future be commensurate with the seriousness of this illness in Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION RESPECTING ESSIAC TREATMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and duty to present a petition signed by over 5,580 residents of the riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka. The petitioners are calling upon Parliament to pass into law legislation respecting Essiac. Essiac is a remedy which has had very encouraging effects on cancer patients. My constituents believe that this treatment should be made available across Canada at a reasonable cost for the millions who may suffer from this dreaded disease.
Therefore, the petitioners humbly pray and call upon the House of Commons to ensure that the Government of Canada proceeds swiftly with such legislation.

subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and privilege to present a petition on behalf of a number of residents of the City of Toronto who call on Parliament to raise its voice with respect to the trade deal between Canada and the United States because it would reduce Canada's ability to plan the economic, social, and cultural program which Canadians need; because it would integrate Canada further into the North American defence industrial base; and because they believe that the very fabric of Canadian sovereignty is threatened by the proposed trade deal.
Since the Government had no mandate to negotiate a free trade deal with the United States, they call upon Parliament to ensure that there is a national debate and that this debate results in a national general election before any trade deal with the United States is signed and ratified.
Mr. Speaker, I have two further petitions, also from residents in Toronto and surrounding areas who believe that
the Conservative Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States.
They believe that the promise of secure access to the United States market, which was the key objective in the negotiations, has not been achieved. They fear that hundreds of thousands of jobs in Canada will be affected and they, therefore, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

The petitioners point out to Parliament that the free trade agreement would compromise Canadian sovereignty, that it would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future, and that it would undermine our ability to build a society distinct from the United States. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
That the Main Estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1989, laid
upon the Table, Tuesday, February 23, 1988, less the amounts voted in
Interim Supply, be concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend opposite has asked for a copy of the Bill. It would be our intention to debate the concurrence motion through the day and then move to the Bill. However, as a matter of courtesy, I have absolutely no objection to the Bill being distributed now.
I welcome the opportunity to participate today in the debate on the 1988-89 Main Estimates, because it gives me an opportunity to describe to Hon. Members of the House the broad policy thrusts and the certain specific expenditure measures which are reflected in our spending plans. The Main Estimates, which were tabled in the House by my colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), last February 23, is a clear expression of the Government's commitments- its commitment to controlling expenditure growth, its commitment to increasing public service efficiency, and its commitment to introducing new initiatives which respond to the needs of Canadians in a number of high priority areas.
The spending plans which are detailed in these Estimates confirm the Government's ongoing commitment to its program of economic renewal. It is a program which we firmly believe
Supply
could only be successfully implemented if we regain control of the federal Government's fiscal situation.
Details of our spending plan highlight the successes we have achieved in our sustained and continuing efforts to reverse the previously uncontrolled spending growth and ever-rising deficits and to make public sector management more responsive and productive.
We believe that results matter more than good intentions, and it is specifically about results I wish to speak today. The total budgetary Main Estimates of $119.4 billion are 7.7 per cent higher than the comparable Estimates of the previous fiscal year. In addition to Main Estimate expenditures, which are by far its largest component, the Government's total spending plan for 1988-89 includes reserves for Supplementary Estimates to be brought to Parliament during the course of the year, and certain expenditures that will be financed through separately funded special purpose accounts or will arise from the re-evaluation of the Government's assets and liabilities.
The 7.7 per cent increase in the Main Estimates over last year is fully covered in the 5.5 per cent growth in planned budgetary spending for the year. The growth in the Main Estimates is larger than originally targeted for total spending for the year because the Government has included more of its new initiatives in this year's Main Estimates than it was able to do last year. This means that fewer resources will be needed for adjustments during the year through the course of Supplementary Estimates.
Total budgetary expenditures in 1988-89 are forecast at SI32.3 billion. That is an increase of 5.5 per cent over the estimated expenditures of $125.3 billion in 1987-88.
I want to point out to the House that while those numbers may not seem very impressive, what is impressive is that since 1984-85 the average annual increase in budgetary expenditures has been 4.9 per cent. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to contrast this to the average increases of more than 15 per cent a year over the preceding five-year period of the previous administration which was in control of government spending. In fact, if one excludes public debt charges built on the deficits of the previous years and focuses exclusively on program expenditures, the average increase is only 3.7 per cent between 198586 and 1988-89. That is less than the rate of inflation over the same period and a mere fraction of the average annual increases between 1980-81 and 1984-85 which ran at more than 14 per cent.
When we took office in the fall of 1985, we launched a three-part strategy for economic renewal. It was focused first on restoring fiscal responsibility, second on removing obstacles to growth, and third on encouraging new investment.
As part of the first strategy, we realized the pressing need to reduce the size of the deficit in an orderly, balanced, and fair manner and to control the growing burden of the public debt.
Our first priority in achieving these goals was to get spending under control. I believe the results to date and the
COMMONS DEBATES_________________ June 27, 1988
Supply
intentions set out by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), in his last Budget provide ample proof of our achievements and continuing resolve.
In 1984-85, after five years of uninterrupted increases, budgetary expenditures peaked at nearly 25 per cent of Canada's Gross Domestic Product. Since then budgetary expenditures have consistently declined as a share of the Gross Domestic Product. For the current fiscal year these expenditures are forecast to represent 22.5 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product and, as my colleague, the Minister of Finance, indicated in his medium term projections in the February Budget, their proportion is expected to decline substantially to just over 19 per cent by 1992-93.
Not since the late 1970's have the federal Government's expenditures consistently represented less than 20 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product. Our determined and unrelenting efforts to control expenditures have paid off. They have paid off with increased prosperity and decreased pressures on the Treasury.
Reduced expenditure growth, along with increased revenues, largely the result of greater economic activity across Canada, have led to systematic reductions in the deficit. While it is not where we want it yet, there is no question that the trend line is positive.
With budgetary expenditures of some SI32 billion and revenues of over $103 billion, the projected deficit for 1988-89 is less than $29 billion. That is a reduction of $9.4 billion over 1984-85 when it was a massive, unworkable $38.3 billion.
Our commitment to controlling expenditures, reducing the size of the deficit, and responding to the needs of Canadians in a challenging and changing environment shows in the major elements of the 1988-89 Main Estimates.
Of the $119.4 billion in total budgetary Main Estimates, $78.5 billion or two-thirds are for statutory programs. The remainder, some $40.9 billion, is what is included in the appropriation Bill to be approved at the end of today.
More than 90 per cent of statutory spending is by four Departments: Finance, Health and Welfare, Employment and Immigration, and Secretary of State.
These statutory expenditures include public debt charges, major transfer payments to individuals, transfers to provinces, grants to municipalities, the Government's contribution to the unemployment insurance account, and agricultural and transportation subsidies.
Public debt charges at $32.1 billion are the largest single component of expenditures. They represent 41 per cent of the statutory spending and nearly one-quarter of the Government's total projected spending in 1988-89. That is the legacy left to us by the previous Government. The increase of nearly $3.9 billion in these charges accounts for approximately two-thirds of the total increase in statutory estimates.
Other statutory payments, such as transfers to the provinces and territories for hospital insurance, medicare, extended health care, post-secondary education, and social assistance and services, are all projected to rise this year. Federal Government cash payments to the provinces for health and post-secondary education are included in the Main Estimates at just over $9.4 billion, an increase of some $200 million over 1987-88.
Canada Assistance Plan payments, covering half the cost of provincial social assistance and social services for people in need, will amount to nearly $4.5 billion in 1988-89. That is a $280 million increase over last year.
Fiscal transfer payments, contained principally in the estimates of the Department of Finance, are made up essentially of the unconditional fiscal equalization payments to the poorer provinces. These are expected to rise by over $800 million in this year.

In addition to these cash payments from the federal Government, the provincial Governments will benefit from fiscal transfers that should exceed $9 billion in 1988-89. Thus, federal assistance for health care, education, welfare and other public services should total nearly $30 billion this year.

Nearly $1 billion has been added to this year's Estimates to meet the higher benefit payments to Canada's elderly under Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement. These increases are the result of two factors-higher monthly payments indexed to changes in consumer prices and the growth in the size of the eligible population. Combined income support payments to Canada's elderly will account for $15.5 billion in expenditures this year. They represent the second largest component of the Government's total spending plan.
Since taking office our Government has introduced a number of measures to improve the incomes of elderly Canadians. These have included modifications to the rules governing private pension plans, among them higher RRSP contribution levels,-

The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) has arrived. It is nice to see you here, Sir.
In that regard I would remind the House that we extended the spouses' allowances program to cover low-income widows and widowers between the ages of 60 years to 64 years, a move
June 27, 1988

that increased benefits to a great number of elderly Canadians, the majority of whom were women.
I want to turn now to the voted expenditures. Over one-quarter of the nearly $40.9 billion in voted expenditures contained in the 1988-89 Main Estimates will be made by the Department of National Defence. The remaining 75 per cent or $30.6 billion is some $1.5 billion or 5.3 per cent higher than last year's corresponding amount. The annually voted expenditures category, in addition to containing the costs associated with the operations of government, also includes the costs of several new initiatives to respond to the pressing needs of Canadians announced by the Government over the past year.
I want to detail some of these initiatives, if I may. They include the $306 million for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. That Bill is presently held up in the Senate. We certainly hope that it will be released by the Senate so that we can do for the Atlantic provinces what my good friends opposite know should be done. It is unfortunate that it is delayed there. We hope my friends opposite will use their best efforts with the Liberal Senators to free that particular Bill as soon as possible.
There is $312 million for the Western Diversification Office and $197 million in increased regional development funding for regions such as northern Ontario.
The Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the Western Diversifiation Fund include the 1988-89 portions of the Government's $1.5 billion and $1.2 billion five-year commitment to the Atlantic and western regions. With these and other regionally directed initiatives this Government will continue to promote the diffusion of economic well-being to all areas of Canada.
Excluding the almost one-half billion dollars in incremental funding for these new agencies and the voted expenditures of defence, the remaining annual appropriations in the Main Estimates exhibit an annual increase of only 3.6 per cent, which is below the projected increase in consumer prices. We have been able to achieve this lower growth in voted programs by reducing the cost of program delivery, on the one hand, and by curtailing and eliminating programs that have outlived their usefulness, on the other.
Reduced program delivery costs are a direct result of determined efforts to improve management in the federal public sector. Public service managers have been challenged to find ways of improving the productivity of government administration, and the results show that their efforts have been successful. Operations throughout government have benefited from improvements in both efficiency and effectiveness. High standards of program delivery have been maintained with fewer human and financial resources. I will return to this point in a moment.
I would like to emphasize that our efforts have not been a blind pursuit of lower growth rates in federal expenditures. If we take a look at the details of those expenditures in the 1988-
Supply
89 Main Estimates, along with the record of our actions since September, 1984, we find they clearly show that notwithstanding a determined commitment to control spending growth and reducing the size of the federal deficit, this Government is aware of and responds to the special needs of various groups as and when they occur. Wherever possible, we have reallocated resources to provide better increases than average in certain priority areas.
Over the years these areas have included defence spending, official development assistance funding for regional development, and assistance to particular groups such as Canada's grain producers. With its foreign aid the Government has moved resolutely to give concrete expression to the concerns of Canadians about the peoples of less developed countries.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext: By deferring your commitments?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Deferring our commitments? Is that like saying we are going to stay in NATO for the first term in office and then get out the second term? Would that be a deferral? Would you like to ponder that for a moment?
Canada's Official Development Assistance in 1988-89 is expected to reach nearly $2.9 billion. This represents an increase of 8.3 per cent over 1987-88. In the four years since 1984-1985 Canada's Official Development Assistance is up by nearly $800 million or 37.3 per cent. These increases clearly reflect our Government's determination to meet Canada's commitment to maintain Official Development Assistance at one-half of one per cent of Gross Domestic Product to the end of the decade.
Our international development and assistance efforts have been strengthened by decisions to provide all financial assistance in the form of grants rather than concessional loans, to declare a debt moratorium in favour of sub-Saharan African countries, and to put in place the Caribcan agreement. This particular agreement recognizes that Canada has a special relationship with the Commonwealth Caribbean countries. Among other things, it provides them with duty-free access to our market for a number of specified goods.
The budgetary Main Estimates for defence at $11.2 billion are projected to increase by $860 million or 8.3 per cent over the 1987-88 Main Estimates. This increase is essential if Canada is to meet its sovereignty objectives, honour its international defence commitments within NATO and NORAD, and promote international stability by providing military assistance to United Nations sponsored peacekeeping operations.
Re-equipment and modernization of the Canadian Armed Forces, priorities of this Government, are proceeding in a staged and orderly manner. Some $188 million of the total increase of the budget of the Department of National Defence has been allocated to capital. At nearly $3 billion in 1988-89, National Defence's capital budget is intended to support normal capital and construction requirements and to contribute to the costs of major capital acquisition programs. I am

June 27, 1988
Supply
referring to the Canadian Patrol Frigate Program, the Low Level Air Defence System, the Tribal Class Update and Modernization Program, North American air defence modernization, and the CF-18 fighter aircraft. This much needed re-equipment and increase in the size of the Forces will serve to meet our goal of enhancing the operational effectiveness of the Canadian Armed Forces and maintaining a strong defence capability.
The Main Estimates are full of other examples that demonstrate how the Government has been able to reallocate resources to respond to those priority areas it has identified. I would like to describe a few of these examples briefly, for the benefit of my colleagues.
If there is one area of economic progress about which we are particularly pleased, it is in the creation of jobs. Since the Government took office 1.3 million jobs have been created, and we are continuing to devote considerable funds to the Canadian Jobs Strategy, a comprehensive approach to training and job creation which we adopted in the summer of 1985. Our goals are to create lasting employment and to increase the level of skills of Canadian workers.
If I may just digress from my notes, Mr. Speaker, the interesting thing to note is that 87 per cent of the jobs which we have created have been full-time jobs, whereas 80 per cent of the jobs created by the previous administration were parttime ones.
I appreciate that I am drawing to the end of my time.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to reply to the Minister. He has just taken the opportunity to recount the progress that the Government has made in accordance with its policy measures. He made two points to which I wish to refer.
The Minister talked about getting the debt under control. One of the main objectives of the Government has been to get the debt under control. The question is: Who has borne the burden of getting it under control?
I submit that it is those people and those areas of the country which can least afford to bear that burden. I say that because if government programs are cut everyone is not equally affected. The people who are affected most are those who depend on government programs.
Which parts of the country depend on government programs? It is those less developed areas of the country which depend on them. I submit that when cuts are made in transport, fisheries, and in programs of the Government of Canada in terms of transfer payments, those areas of the country that have weak private sectors and which depend on government programs are impacted upon negatively.
It is all very well to talk about getting the debt under control, but if we look behind the lines and read between the lines-which is a rather mixed metaphor; one cannot do both at the same time-we see that getting the debt under control has been borne by those people in the country who can least afford to bear it.
Let me take an example to consider. The Minister talked about an increase in EPF, which is true. However, what is the increase? The increase is 5 per cent, whereas there was a signed agreement between the Government of Canada and the provinces to increase EPF by 7 per cent. Thus over $1 billion less was going to the provinces for post-secondary education and health than was anticipated. All of that will have to come out of the provincial budgets which will impact on students, young people who have the highest unemployment rate of any sector in the population in the country. For example, in the Province of Newfoundland, according to Statistics Canada, youth unemployment is close to 50 per cent. That is the type of impact that there is on the regions when government programs are cut.
I wish to make some comments about another point that the Minister made, that is, the removal of obstacles to growth. I want to take this opportunity to dwell on it at length, because we do not get very many opportunities in the House to talk about things that are important to our areas and to us. The Government just removed what it thought was an obstacle to growth. It was called the Newfoundland Railway. I want to comment on the amount of dollars that were allocated to that province in supposed compensation for what was considered to be an obstacle to growth.
The post-mortems are just starting to come in on that particular move by the Government of Canada. Here is what The Sunday Express stated yesterday in the province. It polled the other Maritime provinces to see how they felt about what had happened. Mr. MacKenzie, Director of the Transportation Division for the Prince Edward Island Government, said:
I guess most people feel that when they look at the $800 million figure,
Newfoundland has been dealt with generously. However when you stop to
analyse it, it is not such a great deal.
The other provinces are now looking at the deal and saying that it is not a good one and that, in fact, the Province of Newfoundland has been sold out. It has been sold out in what
June 27, 1988

The Sunday Express called "The great train robbery". This is an example of getting the public debt under control and removing obstacles to growth. This is what was written in The Sunday Express about the latest measure taken by the Government of Canada:
Why should Newfoundlanders have to trade their railway in order to get an upgraded Trans-Canada Highway? No other part of the country had to face that demeaning choice. Following the same logic, will Ottawa suggest, and the province meekly agree somewhere down the road, that Newfoundlanders must accept cuts in their postal service in order to upgrade their ferry service. Will improved air service be linked to cutbacks in the RCMP? Absurd, yes, but it is exactly what happened in the closure of the Newfoundland railway.
No other province has had to do that. No other province will do it. New Brunswick says that it wants $1 billion to upgrade its portion of the Trans-Canada Highway, but Premier McKenna will not be bargaining away the province's main rail lines to get it. He said that they would never sign a deal like the one Premier Peckford agreed to.
The Sunday Express went on to state:
The great train robbery has not gone unnoticed in Newfoundland. The road-builders association sees the deal as too little too late. As a short term analysis of the situation that is a devastating indictment. Port aux Basques fears for its civic life, and rightfully so; seven million dollars can never replace the towns raison d'etre. From cabin owners who will now not be able to reach their summer places, to ordinary citizens who realize that something has been taken from the province that every other Canadian province takes for granted, there is an oceanic sense that politicians have sold the province out.
What are the factors here? First, there was an obligation, a constitutional obligation on the part of the Government of Canada. What was stated in the Terms of Union in 1949 when we joined this country was that the Government of Canada would relieve the province of the burden of providing a transportation system up to national standards. That is what was written in the Constitution of Canada according to the Terms of Union which was signed in 1949.
In 1949 there were no roads.

speechtext:
The Bullet stayed and Liberal Governments not only maintained the Bullet but built roads. It was the Pearson Government that built and constructed totally the Trans-Canada Highway across the Island of Newfoundland. That is what the Pearson Government did.
It was the Trudeau Government that started the TransLabrador Highway. So road-building has gone on under other programs, not in a trade for the railway but under other programs of the Government of Canada. For example, there was the Atlantic Development Agency going back to the 1960s, and then after that there was DREE. More recently there was the Department of Economic and Regional Development. All these agencies of the Government of Canada had built roads in areas where they were needed without any trade

for the railroad. But this particular Government has said: "If you want to go on building roads now and in the future you must trade your railway for that".
What does the trade involve? What do we get in the trade? We get $700 million in federal dollars over 15 years. This is how the Government of Canada reduces debts. This is how it removes obstacles to growth. We got $700 million over 15 years. After 15 years that is the end. That has never happened before. When John Diefenbaker dealt with term 29 involving transfer payments to the province, he agreed that there was an obligation in perpetuity, not ending after 15 years. Here we get $700 million over 15 years. What does that involve? The Government of Canada was paying $40 million a year to support the Newfoundland Railway anyway. I was never strong on math, and it is a wonder therefore that I was ever appointed Minister of Revenue, but if I divide 15 into 700 it is approximately $46 million a year. The Government of Canada was paying $40 million a year anyway, and what we are getting is $46 million a year. The Minister of International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) has bargained for an additional $6 million a year, the $6-million man. That is what is happening. I do not see how anybody in his right mind can say that that is a fair, just, and equitable deal for the province.
Out of that $700 million how much is going into the area of Labrador? Twelve million dollars is going into the TransLabrador Highway, an extremely important initiative for that particular area of the country. It does not have a train except the one built by the company that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was formerly president of-the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway which is a private operation. Apart from that there are no trains at all. We do have the start of a highway system. What did the Government of Canada do? It put $12 million into the Trans-Labrador Highway which is less than was put in in 1983. When that road was started in 1983, $14 million was allocated. If one adds inflation to $14 million, one gets probably twice as much as the $12 million that was allocated under this particular deal.
That is what we get in exchange for that trade-away. That is what we get in spite of the fact that the Sullivan Commission, which was set up to recommend on the terms of phasing out the railroad, said that one of the conditions should be building a road across Labrador. What did Sullivan actually say? He made many important recommendations. He recommended the termination of the Newfoundland Railway, and no one is objecting to that. What we are objecting to is the terms of how the railway is being terminated.
Sullivan recommended the termination of the Newfoundland Railway in return for appropriate guarantees for alternate federal commitments to provide transportation service; the upgrading of the Trans-Canada Highway; the strengthening of the role of direct water shipments, port development in St. John's, Corner Brook, and in the Baie d'Espoir area; improvements to air services to remote communities on the

June 27, 1988
Supply
coast of Labrador, which is already being done at the cost of some $40 million; and a total transportation plan for Labrador to support resource development. That included the building of the Trans-Labrador Highway from the Straits of Belle Isle through Goose Bay and on to Labrador West. None of that has been addressed in this particular transportation package. What we have received is a token amount of $12 million, nothing at all close to what Sullivan recommended.
Again, I point out that this is a trade in spite of the obligation of the Government of Canada. At the present time the Government is spending money to sell this deal. This deal is so bad that there is a necessity to have a public information program, and ads are now being published in newspapers to tell the people how good this deal really is. If some of that money could be used to build roads or to advance the cause of the Trans-Labrador Highway, how much better off would we be?
The post-mortem is still not complete on this particular deal. What we are hearing so far, from those who build roads and from those who use them, is that this is absolutely and completely inadequate and a total sell-out as far as the Province of Newfoundland is concerned.
In terms of the record of this particular Party, we have always taken the position that one does not trade one for the other. One builds the roads and the railway exists at the same time. It was the Pearson Government who built the Trans-Canada Highway in Newfoundland, and it was the Trudeau Government who allocated the first funds for the construction of the Trans-Labrador Highway. Our position as a Party is that that type of policy must continue.
If we were the Government of Canada, here is what we would have done; if we become the Government of Canada, here is the position that we will take. We would consider respect number one for constitutional obligations. We would not hold the people of Newfoundland and Labrador liable for the signatures on Section 10(1) of the Memorandum of Understanding which relieves Canada of all constitutional obligations with respect to the Newfoundland Railway.
It is one thing to build a road, but how is that road maintained? The Government of Newfoundland has the least fiscal capacity of any Government in this country. Yet the Government of Canada now states that it wants to build a Cadillac road and not give the province a Chevette maintenance plan, not give any maintenance plan at all. How will that province maintain such a highway once it is built?
We think that the Government of Canada must continue its constitutional obligations, not only to build a transportation system of national standards, but to maintain a transportation system of national standards, whether it be rail or road.
Second, we think that there should be an amendment to the Terms of Union to transfer Canada's constitutional obligations to the Newfoundland Railway to a new federal obligation to maintain the Trans-Canada Highway. We recognize that the
present financial compensation package is grossly inadequate. We believe that there should be a renegotiating to a more realistic and equitable financial package for the people of the province. We recognize that the present financial compensation of $15 million for community adjustment is totally inadequate. We believe that this amount should be renegotiated with the provincial Government in consultation with those communities affected by the closure of the railway. We believe in the principle of the reconstruction of the Trans-Canada Highway. In that regard we see the Labrador highway as an integral part of any such highway system. We believe that federal funding must be made available for its completion.
This railroad has been phased out without putting any roads in its place. What is now happening is that the railroad is going as of September 1; as of September there will be no more railroad in Newfoundland, yet the reconstruction of the highway does not start until 1991. In other words, the Government of Canada is taking something away before it has even started to put something else in its place.
For all those reasons, we can only condemn this particular initiative on the part of the Government of Canada. First, it does not meet the Government's constitutional obligation. Second, it treats Newfoundland differently from any other province in that it asks it to trade a railroad for another system of transportation. Third, the package is completely inadequate and does not address the needs of the whole province, particularly the area of Labrador which will receive 2 per cent or $ 12 million of the total package in order to construct the Labrador highway, and it does not nearly meet the recommendations of the Sullivan Commission set up to advise on the phase out of the Newfoundland Railway.
Truly the Government of Canada has the debt of the country under control, and truly it is removing obstacles to growth. However, the unfortunate thing is that the Government is doing that on the backs of those people of the regions of Canada who can least afford to bear it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to talk a bit about the Estimates. This is a frustrating exercise. We are now being asked to consider Estimates of over $100 billion and to do so in a very short period of time, according to a time honoured ritual, one which in my opinion does not give adequate scope for Members of the House of Commons to get into the nitty-gritty of the Estimates of individual Departments.
I am a Member of Parliament who has had a great deal of experience at the provincial level as well. As such, I believe that when we look at the reform of the rules of the House of Commons anew as we should after the next election, in addition to the general discussions of policy, there should be opportunity for the different committees to look more specifically at the spending of the different Departments. In my view the current situation is not satisfactory. Ministers are expected
June 27, 1988

to defend their Estimates for a matter of a couple of hours before a committee and then are expected to do no more.
The Estimates represent the heart of the priority setting exercise of any Government. We are not at all at ease with the priorities of this particular Government. We will oppose the Bill which will be coming forward this afternoon for concurrence in the Estimates because we are very disturbed at the directions taken by the Government in economic management and in spending. As I have suggested, I think that there must be a better way. I believe as well that there must be a way for Parliament to look at spending without the Government simply saying that this is a matter of confidence and therefore no change, no scrutiny, and no information will be provided in any meaningful way.
I think we have moved a fair distance since 1984 when the Government indicated that the deficit above all would be the priority for the Progressive Conservative Government. There has been some economic recovery since that time, but it has been largely concentrated in central Canada and, more specifically, in southern Ontario. If I travel 25 miles outside my constituency of Ottawa Centre, I begin to see the problems of the other Canada, those Canadians who do not have access to job opportunities in the way those in southern Ontario have started to have.
The Government has taken the view that it is all hunky-dory. It seems to have taken the view that because things have started to move in southern Ontario, things are under control and it does not need to worry about the rest of the country. The Government has also changed its view with respect to the importance of bringing down the deficit.
Hon. Members will recall the rhetoric that came from both the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) when they were talking about economic renewal and about bringing changes into force in a way "that is fair, open and consistent with the basic sense of compassion, tolerance and justice that is characteristic of Canadian society". They said in 1984 that "we will not weaken the basic income support programs that have served Canadians well. Indeed, we will seek to provide even greater assistance to those Canadians who truly need it".
You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that it was not long after that that the Government began its effort to try to undermine the basic income support for senior citizens by deindexing old age pensions. I was struck by the selective amnesia demonstrated by the Government House Leader in his introduction just a few minutes ago. He forgot the Government's efforts to deindex the old age pension, the centre-piece of its 1985 Budget.
I am also struck by the fact that the Government said in 1984 that after two or three years of economic recovery real action would be needed on the deficit. The Government brought the deficit down below the S30 billion mark and then stalled. Perhaps it stalled because of the realities of Canadian politics. Perhaps it ran out of ideological fervour. I am not

quite sure, but it stalled in its attempt to bring the deficit below the $29 billion mark. There was always a reason why it could not be done now. The impact of the Minister of Finance in pursuing that particular quest became less and less until we came to the situation we have seen in recent weeks.
The Government, in some despair, because of the failure of Canadians to respond to its management of the economy, has decided that the way back to power is not by reducing the deficit but is in fact by seeking to spend its way back into the affections of Canadians from coast to coast. After considerable procrastination, a promise was made to help Saskatchewan Francophones. The Government promised $120 million for regional development in Lac-Saint-Jean. After ignoring the needs of this area since 1984, all of a sudden the Conservatives felt it was time to do something.

speechtext:
This is a very serious question in terms of government spending priorities. When the Secretary of State happened to notice and feel a political need, he responded by writing a cheque, and $1.4 million was granted right away.
I spoke to a meeting of the Association of Municipalities of Ontario. Back in 1983 the Federation of Canadian Municipalities came to the Government of Canada-and it has come back every year since-with a request to try to renew the
infrastructure of our Canadian cities and towns. This is a program which has been very carefully costed and thought out, a program which would have the effect of ensuring and putting in place very substantial renewal of roads, sewage systems, recreational facilities, and municipal infrastructure of all kinds in order to maintain our Canadian cities and towns as liveable places for our Canadian families. That is also a program which can be regionally oriented toward areas of high unemployment. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities was looking not for $40 billion, not for $20 billion, not for $16 billion; it was looking for the federal Government to share in a portion of the total costs spent. What happened, Mr. Speaker? The Federation was given the back of the hand from the Government of Canada.
On the other hand, let us look at when a few admirals and generals got going in trying to reorient Canadian defence priorities. Where these cities and towns of Canada could not get the federal Government to share one-third of the $7 billion cost of renewal of infrastructure of Canadians cities and towns over the course of a five or six year period, the admirals and generals were able to get in the defence White Paper a commitment to a new fleet of nuclear submarines, which is currently costed at $8 billion and which every Canadians knows will cost $12 billion or $15 billion or $16 billion before that fleet is built. Over the course of the weekend the Environ-ics poll indicated that support for the proposal had dropped to less than one-third of Canadians and that 60 per cent of Canadians said that $16 billion or $8 billion was too much to spend on the nuclear submarines. Canadians are saying that it is a priority which the Government should drop.
What is happening in this particular Estimates exercise today is quite clear. On the one hand, spending on defence prior to nuclear submarines is going up by $860 million, an increase of 8.3 per cent, the largest percentage increase of any major Department of the Government of Canada. Let us look at the contrast. We spend $800 million or $900 million on defence in 1988-89 while the increase in the budget for CIDA, the Canadian International Development Agency, according to the Estimates, is approximately $122 million. We spend seven times more on defence than we spend on our major aid granting agency, CIDA.
Recently it has come to my attention that the percentage of Canada's Gross National Product going into aid this year is down by a fraction of a per cent from what it was a year ago. Rather than moving steadfastly and determinately to increase our spending on aid, we are reducing it. At the same time the proportion of our GNP which is going into spending on national defence is equally and steadfastly going up year after year after year.
The admirals went public back in 1983 asking for nuclear subs, but have they come back to meet with Cabinet year after year and been turned away? Have they been ignored in their requests? They did not need to because they had the inside track. Canada cannot afford to renew a road to a sewage system and that kind of thing. The federal Government turns

its back on the efforts of Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton to renew the Green Creek collector sewage treatment system here in my City of Ottawa, yet it can come up with $8 billion nominal and $16 billion in actual terms for the nuclear submarines, infrastructure, training, and other things. A very serious debate is taking place within Cabinet over this issue between the hawks and the doves. As a Canadian, I hope the doves win.
If the doves win it will not, I suspect, mean that the Government will abandon the proposal for nuclear submarines but will mean that the proposal will be stretched out, knowing that a new Government will scrap it because it is unlikely the Conservatives will have a majority after the next general election. As my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), indicated in Thunder Bay over the course of the weekend at the Ontario New Democratic Convention, some priorities once selected by government have to be respected by an opposition Party, but where an opposition Party indicates clearly that it is in fundamental disagreement with a priority of government and will not go along with it, we are entitled to abandon a commitment even if the commitment is signed under contract, which I believe some of the Conservatives want to do. We are making it clear that Canada does not need to spend $16 billion on nuclear submarines. That is not a priority of the New Democratic Party. If we form the next Government of Canada we will scrap that priority; if we are part of the next Government of Canada we will scrap that priority. We will not be a part of that, and 60 per cent of Canadians agree with us that that should not be a priority.

Premier Bourassa and Premier Peterson are objecting to this policy. Not only that, if we ask whether everyone in Toronto is prosperous, the answer is definitely no. They cannot afford the average price of a home which, in the City of Toronto itself, has now risen to more than $200,000. Why do you not join with me and suggest to your erstwhile colleagues on the Conservative side that we take the $16 billion allotted for nuclear subs and use it for child care, for renewing municipal infrastructure, for social services, for adequate postal services, for foreign aid, and for peace and development? My friend from York East has from time to time raised questions about housing. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to speak to the Main Estimates for the year 1988-89, layed upon the table on February 23 by the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mazankowski).
Mr. Speaker, before I start my comments on the Main Estimates, I must say I have just survived one of the most trying 20-minute periods of my life, but I suppose that is the price you pay for democracy. It means listening to silly speeches by people who don't know whether they are coming or going. Every morning I say to myself: Fontaine, you have to put up with the socialists because that's the price you pay for democracy!
June 27, 1988

Mr. Speaker, today we can announce to the people of Canada that we have a balanced budget that is based on Canadians' ability to pay. In fact, the Government, through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), has released information about our tax reform, and today we can inform Canadians that because of the Government's good management, we have been able to control our budget; the annual deficit has declined from $38 billion to $29 billion; and as of July 1, 1988, on the first paycheck of that week, around July 8 or 9, each Canadian will have more money to take home because for the first time since 1917, there will be a significant change in the application of our income tax legislation.
And this is thanks to a Conservative Government, a Government that provides good management. Retroactive to January 1, 9.7 million Canadian households will pay fewer taxes. They will notice it on the paycheck they get around July 8 this year. I say to all Canadians, Mr. Speaker: Around the beginning of July, when you get that additional money in your pockets, remember you are getting it thanks to the good management of the Progressive Conservative Party. And 850,000 Canadians will no longer pay income tax. This again is thanks to good management, and I would also like to take this opportunity to congratulate my colleague, the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald). Because of this Government's excellent management, the Minister was able to find more money so that she could announce to Canadians how we can further enhance our culture and our Canadian identity and how the CBC will protect that culture and give all Canadians a chance to enjoy its benefits.
If we hadn't put a stop to the reckless spending of the previous Government, the Minister of Communications would never have been able to table that kind of legislation today.
Mr. Speaker, what else did we do? But first I would like to comment on what was said by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). During his 20 minutes, the Hon. Member attacked my riding in a very destructive way when he said, and his Leader and his Party have said the same: "No submarines for Canadians." And we all know that the riding of Levis will be able to live on this magnificent Government contract for twenty-five years.
I find it particularly annoying to be faced daily, both in this House and in the media, with negative comments on the greater Quebec City area and on the province of Quebec, because it is a fact that the submarines will have to be built in the province of Quebec.
When Members of the other Party, the socialists, tell us this would cost $16 billion, that is just not true, Mr. Speaker. Experts with the Department of the National Defence have told us the submarines would cost $8 billion, and $8 billion spread over twenty-five years is $300 million annually, while in Canada, we spend $60 billion annually on social benefits.
This means that the budget for submarines is 0.5 per cent of the amount spent annually on social affairs in this country. So
Supply
when we are accused of spending indecently, the representatives of the socialist party should once again explain their position to the people.
I also want to point out a comment on the by-election in Lac-Saint-Jean made by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre. Mr. Speaker, the result in Lac-Saint-Jean is a real opinion poll, a wonderful sampling of public opinion. In Lac-Saint-Jean, we saw the socialist candidate, who we must admit was an intelligent man, a local man, a scientist involved in the community, a son of a former mayor, a union activist in a region where there are many unions. So in theory, he had everything going for him, Mr. Speaker, but he did not even get enough votes to avoid losing his deposit. That is the real opinion poll and that is what the members of the socialist Party deserved.
That is the message they deserved to get from Canadians. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, another by-election was being held in Quebec, in the riding of Anjou, and there, one of the candidates, the socialist candidate-we know that the socialist Party does not distinguish between the provincial Party and the federal Party, it is the national party throughout the country; it was a candidate from this Party who ran for the thirteenth time in Anjou, and the thirteenth consecutive defeat for Mr. Morin, the socialist candidate in Anjou! He got less than 2 per cent of the votes, about 440 votes. This shows that the public has had enough of this party's wild ideas. This shows that the people see that for the past two weeks, this Party has used the time of the House of Commons in a completely disagreeable, shameful way, by proposing Bills whose only purpose is to take up the time of this House and delay our free trade legislation.
And here too, I comment on a remark made by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, who unfortunately has left, Mr. Speaker, to the effect that there are two Canadas. Two Canadas-that makes me think of the official position of Bob White, President of the United Auto Workers, in the riding of Oshawa. Bob White is the one who takes money from the workers to finance the socialist Party. So the definition of Canada that Bob White and the Hon. Member for Oshawa have is really two Canadas: there is Oshawa and southern Ontario where free trade has been in effect successfully since 1965, resulting in $30 billion of sales to the United States, and the rest of Canada, where these people, the highly paid United Auto Workers, do not want all Canadians to benefit from free trade, from the Atlantic to the Pacific. So they are the ones who have a vision of two Canadas: a rich and powerful Canada in Oshawa and a relatively poor Canada in all other parts of this country.
Mr. Speaker, I come back to our legislative effort and budgetary control. Our budget has increased at a rate of 5.5 per cent since 1984, which is very different from the 15 per cent in the years before we came to power. Our Government's expenditures have increased at less than the rate of inflation. That means that our expenses have been cut, which is all the more difficult because many of our expenditures are statutory.

June 27, 1988
Supply
For example, we spend $60 billion for social affairs and we can do very little about that.
There is also interest expense. You know that when we took power, our Government was $200 billion in debt. The interest alone on that was $20 billion. Today, debt service amounts to nearly $30 billion because we got into the habit of spending unaccountably when the Liberals tried to govern this country.
We have also established a number of priority areas. For instance, spending cuts do not mean that the elderly should benefit less from our collective wealth. We have decided to send a clear message to the elderly. They will not be allowed to suffer the negative impact of a difficult financial situation in this country. In fact, the $60 billion available for the elderly, the disabled, young people, and federal participation in provincial social programs will be maintained.
However, we have tried to stop the incredible growth of our bureaucracy by aiming for leaner government. The Liberals tried to create Crown corporations that would compete with the State. Under this Government, the role of the State is to distribute our collective wealth, but the State will no longer compete with the private sector. That is why, for instance, we have divested the Government of corporations like de Havil-land and Canadair. At the time, these companies were responsible for spending not millions but billions of dollars. These billions were borrowed and handed over to administrators who were accountable to Parliament, not to shareholders. They were accountable to something that to them was very remote, and that is why Crown corporations have never made a profit. That is why we decided to privatize them, to return them to the private sector where they will be responsible to their shareholders and will have an obligation to make a profit.
When a Government decides to privatize, it is sending a message that the State is now a partner in the distribution of wealth and no longer competing with the private sector, because it is wrong for the State to compete with private enterprise. It is wrong for a company that manufactures aircraft to compete with a private company that also manufactures aircraft and has to make a profit, while the other company can ask Parliament for funds at the end of each year. That is why we are turning over manufacturing and services to the private sector.
The purpose of our program to enhance productivity within the Government and the public sector is to regain control over the growth of government spending, improve labour relations, negotiate responsible collective bargaining agreements, restructure the supply of government services, review activities to determine the function of the private sector, abolish undue regulatory contraints and reduce the paper burden on the private sector, introduce a better management philosophy-I will get back to all these topics later on, Mr. Speaker-and give managers increased responsibility so they can be more effective.
I referred to controlling the growth of government spending and the public sector, and I must say that, since 1974, the number of public service employees has never been as low as it is now. In fact, in 1984 we told Canadians that the Canadian public service had to be trimmed of its "excess fat". The departments have 235,000 employees, and we thought that an initial reduction of 15,000 was necessary. We also reduced the rate of growth of expenditures, as I said earlier, to a level below the inflation rate.
Labour relations have improved. Since 1986, sixty collective agreements were signed involving annual increases of 3.6 per cent, which compares favourably with the private sector and the provinces, where the average was, respectively, 3.3 and 4.7 per cent. Why is this, Mr. Speaker? Because we feel that public servants should be treated the same way as people who work in private enterprise; we owe it to people in private enterprise who, for all practical purposes, create our collective wealth. Why should we give the public sector preferential treatment, since wealth must first be created by private enterprise, by those who manufacture, provide services, trade, hire Canadians and pay taxes, which are later used to pay Public Servants?
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, we have a new agreement for some 180,000 public servants. We shall try to settle it by negotiating and our goal is a negotiated settlement, not an imposed one, so that we can continue to enjoy excellent working relations with our Public Service and so that Public Servants will be motivated to do excellent work for us.
Another thing we did, Mr. Speaker, was to restructure the provision of government services. In many cases, Canadians who needed government services obtained them at a price that was clearly insufficient and less than the cost of production. That means that if I needed information from Statistics Canada, I obtained it at a lower cost, but I was in a way being subsidized by the taxes of other Canadians to have access to this source of information.
So we have increasingly asked our officials to evaluate the cost of the services provided by the Government and to set the rates accordingly so that those who really benefit from these services pay for them.
We have also sent a message to private enterprise about the burden of procedures and regulations they have to bear. We have put in place systems that put the burden of proof on the Minister before new regulations or procedures can be implemented.
Previously, a Minister would decide one morning to impose additional regulations on Canadians, to impose additional costs on them and often excessive production costs, although this contributed nothing to the community. That is not possible anymore, because the Minister has first of all to prove to his colleagues on the Treasury Board that he was justified in asking for additional funds and in laying down new regulations applying to Canadians.
June 27, 1988

For example, the 15 000 different forms Employment and Immigration Canada was using before 1984 are now down to 3 500. This means a very sizeable decrease in the costs the firms had to incur in order to fill those forms. All our efforts serve that purpose. That is why we are able each year to reduce our operational deficit.
Finally, we have changed our managerial philosophy. In the past, everything in the federal Government was controlled by the Treasury Board and a handful of ministers. For every administrative matter, the rest of the ministers had to consult with the Treasury Board, and to ask permission. It was the same story inside the departments, whether it be the deputy Minister, the directors generals, or even the specialists dealing with a particular file. In no way was it possible to give greater accountability to civil servants.
Now that we have changed that philosophy, the departments are more autonomous, and the Government does not audit the means, but rather the results. The liberals, while they were in power, would never have developed such a concept, it would never have crossed their minds. They were evaluating the means, with no consideration whatsoever for the results.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for all these reasons, we can say that our Government is gradually regaining control over its budget. I will conclude by saying that we went from a deficit of 38 billion dollars a year in 1984, which would be 50 billion dollars this year if the Liberals were still in power, to an annual deficit of 29 billion dollars this year. We succeeded in reducing the deficit and we will continue doing it. Today, we ask the two Opposition parties to speed up the process so that we can vote on these Estimates.

speechtext:
Questions and comments? Debate.
Hon. Warren AUmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of State for the Treasury Board (Mr. Lewis) was speaking this morning, he patted himself on the back for having cut government spending. What the Minister did not say was that very often the wrong programs were cut. He did not point out how this Government promised to spend approximately $165 million to win the by-election in Lac-Saint-Jean, nor did he explain in detail why the Government will spend over $10 billion to purchase nuclear submarines while at the same time cut programs for employment and training by 32 per cent since 1984. This Government has cut a budget which stood at $2.2 billion in 1984 to $1.5 billion in 1988.
The principal program for training and employment under this Government is the Canadian Jobs Strategy. In the Estimates before us today the Government has made a cut in employment and training in real dollars of $125 million from last year. That is a cut of 7.3 per cent. However if we add in the inflation component, the fact that inflation has increased
Supply
by 4 per cent to 5 per cent between 1987 and 1988, that cut amounts to 11 per cent or approximately $188 million. The Government is making cuts such as that while we still have over one million Canadians unemployed.
In a Gallup poll survey taken in this month of June, the following question was asked of Canadians: "What do you believe the biggest single problem in this country to be?" Well, 27 per cent of all Canadians felt that unemployment was the single largest problem in the country. That stood well ahead of 14 per cent who believed that inflation or the economy was a major problem. If we look at the breakdown in those figures we note that in Atlantic Canada 57 per cent thought that unemployment was the major problem, in Quebec it was 26 per cent, on the Prairies it was 31 per cent, and in British Columbia it was 37 per cent. It was only in Ontario that it was not considered to be a major problem.
Why do Canadians feel this way if the Government is doing such a wonderful job with employment? Day after day it brags about the jobs it has created and how the unemployment rate has come down. Canadians feel this way because these figures, which are quoted very often by the Government, are an illusion and do not tell the whole story. To begin with, the great majority of those new jobs have been created in Ontario, particularly in southern Ontario. I do not have the up-to-date figures for this year, but in 1987 more than 95 per cent of the additional jobs created in that year were located in the Province of Ontario.
In an article in Le Devoir French business counsellors are advising business investors in France to invest in Ontario and not in Quebec. The headline in Le Devoir reads:

Quebec is no longer with it, it is now in Ontario that we must invest. [English]
That is one reason Canadians feel that unemployment is still the major problem. The great decrease in unemployment has taken place in Ontario. It has not taken place in Atlantic Canada, in most parts of Quebec, in British Columbia, and in many parts of the Prairies. Another major reason for the unrest of Canadians with respect to unemployment can be found in a report published last week by the advisory council to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall). The report was tabled on June 22. The opening sentences of the press release relating to the report reads: "The problem of unemployed older workers is becoming more severe as the Canadian population ages and as new technology and other economic factors force older worker lay-offs".
The report goes on to say: "It is evident that the employment situation of older workers, particularly those in the 55 to 64 age group, has not improved since 1985". That is when the same advisory council made a report entitled Older Workers: An Imminent Crisis in the Labour Market. In fact, since that report was published the situation has deteriorated. That is another example of why Canadians are concerned about the

June 27, 1988
unemployment situation. They are concerned because the improvement has basically been in Ontario, but it has not helped older workers.
A third reason is that the improvement has failed to help the youth of the country. Again I quote from a report that was tabled in Quebec at the end of last week. It was published by the La Foundation Rennaissance-Jeunesse au Quebec. The study showed that one out of three unemployed persons in Quebec was between the ages of 14 years and 25 years. While one out of three of every unemployed person in Quebec between those ages only makes up one-fifth of the population in Quebec, the report goes on to say that it is a very serious situation in Quebec.
It is interesting but sad to note that the situation of unemployment among young people in Quebec goes hand in hand with an increase in suicides. A recent report from Quebec points out that there has been an increase of 400 per cent in suicides of those between the ages of 15 years and 20 years of age in the last 10 years. This is a very disturbing figure. One must wonder why the Government is so complacent with those kind of unemployment and suicide figures relating to youths. One would think that instead of cutting training and employment budgets and instead of cutting education budgets, particularly budgets for post-secondary education, the Government would be vastly increasing those budgets.
I note that it is one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I will continue my speech after lunch.

subsubtopic: NON-OBSERVANCE OF SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT CONCEPT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Toronto last week as you know the Summit Leaders endorsed the concept of sustainable development. The United Nations General Assembly did the same last December. Yet, despite having twice endorsed sustainable development, the U.S.A. and the U.K. continue to pollute and dump their acid-rain causing gases on their neighbours. In addition, Italy now sends toxic wastes to Africa. Europe has no pollution control measures on automobiles. Japan continues to hunt whales, while here at home we still over-harvest our resources.
Almost one year ago the National Task Force on Environment and Economy wrote a report. Of the 40 recommendations made, so far none has been implemented. As we all know, actions speak louder than words. To endorse environmentally sustainable economic development is one thing. To implement it is another.
Rhetoric is coming out our ears. What really counts is when the Summit Leaders will start practising what they preach.

Mr. Speaker, there is no question that the medical profession has a long-standing tradition of responsibility for caring for people. However, the medical profession is now in danger of self-destructing unless it ceases to be prostituted to bestow an appearance of supporting the anti-child, non-medical, and non-therapeutic act of abortion.
Conducting abortions in which the patient is not suffering a life-threatening situation has nothing remotely to do with healing, or the healing arts, at whatever stage the pregnancy is terminated. As one doctor stated: "It is now past time for doctors and medicine to dissociate themselves from both abortion on demand and from the abortion of the unborn who are thought to suffer from grave mental or physical disability". This doctor also advocated: "Physicians performing an abortion when the life of the mother is not in jeopardy should have their licence suspended".
There is now an ever-growing list of Doctors for Life who will not perform abortions because they believe that unborn children are, indeed, human beings. It is our hope that more and more doctors will join Doctors for Life for the sake of all our unborn children.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow and Wednesday we see the Conservative propaganda machine in action as the Free Trade Business Opportunity Conferences start in Toronto. "Canadian business," the ad states, "needs to know about the opportunities flowing from..." the U.S. trade deal. So there will be "experts on exports" there, especially the keynote speakers, those well-known trade experts, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. MacDougall).
June 27, 1988

Will they tell their audiences about the tragic loss of independence that this deal would bring Canada? Will they explain how we will not have the right to require performance requirements from foreign firms? Will they explain how U.S. health management companies and labs will get the right to come forth and undercut our not-for-profit health system? Will they explain the risk to our regional development programs?
I bet that the answer is no. The program ends at 3 p.m.- early for a serious export conference, but just in time for television deadlines.

subtopic: RESOURCES REQUIRED FOR MAINTENANCE AND EXPANSION
RESOURCES REQUIRED FOR MAINTENANCE AND EXPANSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the sinews of a nation are its transportation links. We move over 250 billion tons of freight annually over our highways. Over the last 15 years the number of registered trucks per kilometre has nearly doubled.
We expect more from our highways but are spending less. If our highway system is to be kept up to date and expanded, then all levels of government must be prepared to allocate more resources to this end. In particular, funding for roads in the Territories has slowed to a trickle. This is unacceptable in an area where there is a desperate need for new and improved highways.

Mr. Speaker, the whole of Hamilton mourned yesterday when we heard of the death of former Member of Parliament for Hamilton West, Dr. Stan Hudecki. Although Dr. Hudecki was here in Parliament for a period of only four years he touched the city of Hamilton in a much greater way. Dr. Hudecki was well respected throughout the community for his work with St. Joseph's Hospital, and for his strong commitment to his religious and family values.
I can remember knocking on doors with Stan and as we went from house to house, in his stolid way, those of us who knew Stan, would say: "Come on Stan, let's get to the door". Stan would say: "I operated on this woman", or "I knew this man."
He had a reputation in the community that spoke above Party lines. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that he was one of the few Members in the Liberal Party who did not support the repatriation of the Constitution because of his strong belief in the values and the rights of the unborn.
He was a man of principle. Although he was a representative of one particular political Party, he had valour and integrity that rose above Party lines. I see my colleague, the Hon. Member for Muskoka (Mr. Darling), nodding his head.
Stan will be missed. To Leona and family we send our sympathies. He had a strong community and family commitment with literally the whole family behind him. Stan, we will really miss you.

subtopic: F-5 FIGHTER PLANE REPAIR AND UPGRADING CONTRACT
F-5 FIGHTER PLANE REPAIR AND UPGRADING CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the F-5 fighter repair and upgrading contract was awarded to Bristol Aerospace in Winnipeg, Winnipeg was promised a world-wide mandate for upgrading and repair of these airplanes.

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND RAILWAY DISBANDMENT-PROVISIONS OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND RAILWAY DISBANDMENT-PROVISIONS OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Newfoundlanders witnessed the signing, a little over a week ago, of an agreement between the Government of Ottawa and the Government of Newfoundland to phase out of existence totally the 100-year old Newfoundland Railway. This deal was done by putting forward a package of dollars to be spent over 15 years to upgrade the highway, amounting to some $700 million, and to shut down the railway almost immediately, effective September 1, 1988.
Newfoundlanders accept the notion that a railway can be phased out for a better highway system if it is not competitive. What we cannot accept is that the amount of money involved will not upgrade the highway. More important, as part of the deal the Government of Canada forced the Government of Newfoundland, and the Government of Newfoundland accepted this, to give up an obligation under the 1949 Terms of Union between Newfoundland and Canada for the Government in Ottawa to provide part of the cost of a national transportation system in the Province of Newfoundland. Ottawa, with the Government of Newfoundland, negotiated away that obligation under the Terms of Union.
We in this Party do not accept making the poorest province in Canada pay that kind of price for a decent transportation system. We commit ourselves to effecting a constitutional amendment to ensure that that Term of Union of 1949 is protected in the Constitution of Canada.

subtopic: AFTERNOON CLOSURES OF POST OFFICE IN HAMILTON MOUNTAIN RIDING
AFTERNOON CLOSURES OF POST OFFICE IN HAMILTON MOUNTAIN RIDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on three separate occasions last week, Westcliff Mall Post Office in my riding was closed for the afternoon. While this fact may not appear to be of great importance, it was significant to the customers who entered the mall expecting to get services from the post office. There had been no prior notification of the closures and no explanation, just a sign on the window saying "closed".
The two clerks who work in the post office had received a telephone call from their wicket supervisor asking them to close up immediately in order to perform relief work in other parts of the city. What else can this be but a blatant attempt by Canada Post to discredit the service provided by the Westcliff Mall Post Office? Customers entering the mall would understandably become upset when they realized that postal services were not available. It is another example of the corporation's insidious efforts to implement its corporate franchising plan by undermining the image of the Westcliff Mall Post Office.

Mr. Speaker, almost a year ago the Sault Ste. Marie Ship Canal developed a fault which closed it down and resulted in the lay-off of over one dozen employees. The canal has been stabilized but no decision has been made to replace it.
The City of Sault Ste. Marie and other people concerned have called on the Government to replace this major shipping link between Lake Superior and Lake Huron, yet the Government has failed to act. It has not even committed enough money for the engineering to take place to decide whether a project should go ahead. When a decision is finally made it will take over two years for construction.
I call on the Government to make a commitment today not only to do the engineering to determine that the ship canal should be replaced but to go ahead and complete the replacement and rehabilitation of this major tourist and shipping link in Sault Ste. Marie.

subsubtopic: CRIMINAL TRAFFICKING IN KIDNAPPED CHILDREN
speechtext:

This type of crime, in my eyes, is no different from murder. One cannot imagine the anguish, terror, and suffering that the children and families involved go through when these kidnappings occur.
