speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: DROUGHT IN WESTERN PROVINCES-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE REQUESTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. On the one hand, today in Toronto the Prime Minister was talking about world drought, the greenhouse effect, and the problems posed for the entire world by climatic change. On the other hand, Canada has a disastrous drought in western Canada. Twenty-four thousand farmers have left the land in the last year and the Government spends almost three times more on propaganda for its trade deal than it does on a concrete program for western farmers and the drought.
Why doesn't the Government introduce a really comprehensive program to aid the farmers of western Canada who are being driven from the land because of drought?

subsubtopic: DROUGHT IN WESTERN PROVINCES-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE REQUESTED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am really quite surprised by the comment of the Leader of the Opposition because Canadian farmers will be happy to tell him that aid from Ottawa to the agricultural community has increased by about 400 per cent since our Government took office.

subsubtopic: DROUGHT IN WESTERN PROVINCES-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE REQUESTED
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DROUGHT IN WESTERN PROVINCES-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE REQUESTED
speechtext:
With regard to the very special problem of the drought which is debilitating many parts of western
Canada and the industrialized world, the Minister of Agriculture has already put together the first part of an important package to assist farmers. The second is on its way and will be announced just as soon as we can.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister was speaking in general terms about global climatic change in Toronto today. What might have changed is also affecting in a long term way the future of Canadian farmers. Increasing droughts and a hotter world climate are not something the Prime Minister surely discovered today in Toronto. Granted, we cannot solve the problems alone, but there are things that the Government can do for Canadians within our own territory.
Three years ago, during another drought season, I called upon the Government of Canada to promote and present a federal-provincial agricultural disaster relief fund. In response to that, on November 27, 1985, the Minister of Agriculture announced, in his words: "We are working toward having a long term disaster assistance program in place for this year's planting season".
1985 has gone by as well as 1986, 1987, and half of 1988, and we still do not have in place a long-term program for agricultural disaster relief. How is that delay going to be explained to the farmers of western Canada?

Mr. Speaker, we have been working with regard to programs such as soil conservation and water resource management with provincial Governments on behalf of farmers. We have worked very closely with the farm organizations.
I met them again just before the Summit and I believe one of them pointed out publicly that that was the seventh meeting I had held with them since I had become Prime Minister, and that it was the first time the Prime Minister of Canada had held such a series of meetings with agricultural leaders across Canada.
We have provided, as I think we should have, a great amount of assistance with regard to drought, when there were floods, and when the problem of grasshoppers arose in western Canada. We provided the largest single deficiency payment in the history of Canada to the agricultural community.
When the agricultural community has been in difficulty it has known that this Government would respond to assist in its problems. We have in the past and we will again in the future.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is all very well for the Prime Minister to go to Toronto and talk in general global terms about the problem, but western farmers are still awaiting the results of a promise
June 27, 1988

made by his Government two and a half years ago to come up with a long-term drought program.
When I was in Saskatoon last week I received questions which 1 am now going to put to the Prime Minister. Where is the long-term drought assistance program? Where is the support for long-term water storage programs in western Canada? Where are the projects to move water to the drought areas? Where are the programs to move feed to the drought areas? Where are the programs to move cattle to areas outside those areas?
Those are the programs western farmers are asking for and they are not going to be overly impressed by the Prime Minister's speech in Toronto.

Mr. Speaker, my recollection is that in the Prince Albert declaration a little more than four years ago we made some 57 or 58 commitments to western agriculture. We have delivered on between 85 and 90 per cent of the entire package.
Hear, hear!

I do not know, Mr. Speaker, why my right hon. friend suggests that it was inappropriate for me to go to Toronto this morning to discuss the important matters of the environment. Surely he would not disagree with my obligation to do that. We certainly do not do this to the exclusion of the agricultural industry or without profound sympathy for it facing the drought which is affecting Canadian agriculture at the moment.
Even my right hon. friend would not blame me for the drought. I know he blames me for everything else, but even he wouldn't try that one.
Well, it's caused by hot air.
If my hon. friend visited with western farmers he would find that most of them would tell him that this Government has done more for western agriculture than any other Government.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF LIVESTOCK STABILIZATION PROGRAM
REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF LIVESTOCK STABILIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since last fall the moisture reserves in western Canada have been at an alltime low. The Minister of Agriculture has been talking about committee meetings since the first of the year. It is almost the first of July. Many crops are not even being planted this year.
When is the Government going to announce a program for stabilization of the livestock industry? Feed prices are going up. Cattle prices are going down. Western farmers want to know when the Government is going to put in place a livestock stabilization program so that they will know they can keep their herds throughout the summer.
Oral Questions
The Government has been talking about committee meetings and consultations. Western farmers want to know when there will be action.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF LIVESTOCK STABILIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unlike the previous Government, our Government believes in consultation because in the end the results demonstrate its utility.
Some four weeks ago the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister and myself met with our counterparts and industry representatives in Calgary. We worked out a timetable which we have been following very closely since then.
Since those meetings some four weeks ago, industry representatives, in consultation with the federal Government and the provinces, have worked closely on a package that we suspect will be put in place soon. In the meantime, we announced in Calgary some $12 million to assist PFRA, which is part of a long-term strategy to work closely with the cattle industry and effect the transportation of water. In addition, there have been some changes to regulations with respect to crop insurance, which are also designed to meet the needs of the farmers in the short term.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF LIVESTOCK STABILIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we heard the Parliamentary Secretary and the Prime Minister give a recitation of what they are talking about and thinking about. Western Canadians want to know when the Government will act. When will the Government bring in a livestock stabilization program? When will it provide an income tax deferral mechanism for herds that have to be dispersed? When will the Government provide assistance for moving cattle out of the drought area? We want to know when the Government will act. Why does it refuse to act?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the Hon. Member talks about the Government refusing to act, I can only assume he is looking back into history. Unlike that administration, this Government, this Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture and others-
You have been there four years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
-have been working on behalf of Canadian farmers since we were elected in 1984. We will continue to do so.
In addition, there is a crop insurance program that was not in place a year ago.

Twenty-four thousand have left.

June 27, 1988
Oral Questions
Issue the writ.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We are following the advice of people like Stan Wilson, who are giving us a timetable-
Call the election-
Twenty-four thousand have left.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The farmers are looking for action, not for advice such as they are receiving from Hon. Members like those from the Hamilton area.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: This Government has been there on behalf of Canadian farmers in the past and we will continue to be there in the future.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE FOR LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS
REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE FOR LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister said a few weeks ago that something would be done soon about the impact of the drought on western producers. The Parliamentary Secretary said a month ago that something was put in the works and a timetable established.
When I was there two weeks ago, farmers in western Canada were saying that they had been waiting two weeks which, for them, was already two weeks too long in meeting the needs of the cattle producers in particular.
A one-shot deal of perhaps $80 to $100 per head of cattle would cost the federal Government about $100 million now. The federal Government has only spent $12 million since the drought began, to deal with the problem. Will the Government commit itself to a one-time assistance program of $80 to $100 per head now so that western producers can make the decision either to get water and feed to their cattle, or get their cattle to the water and feed? Will the Government make that decision now rather than some point down the road?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE FOR LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the farmers on the Prairies, through their Governments, asked us to respond to very serious problems some time ago with respect to grain production, we responded, as my friend knows, with the largest deficiency payment in the history of Canadian agriculture. So I think that indicates the sensitivity that we try to bring to bear to these very legitimate problems affecting Canadian agriculture.
There is not a problem more legitimate than the one being discussed now and we view it with great care and concern and will continue to do so. My hon. friend, the Parliamentary Secretary, has indicated we are following, with the concurrence of agricultural leaders, a very strict timetable. I can assure my hon. friend that the farmers of Canada who, through no fault of their own, are suffering severely because of
these climatic conditions, will find in the Government of Canada, as they have in the past, a strong friend and ally.

Mr. Speaker, I say to the Prime Minister that the farmers are looking for an immediate answer to their needs. The Prime Minister referred to the large deficiency payment the Government granted. He did not mention this announcement was made in the middle of a Saskatchewan election.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: It was delivered, Ed.

Considering the Government did not hesitate to promise to spend $163 million to the voters in the by-election at Lac-Saint-Jean recently, will the Government commit itself to what would amount to $63 million less than this amount for all four of the western provinces affected in this particular circumstance? Will the Government spend that money now when it is needed instead of waiting for byelections to be called in every region across western Canada?
Mr. Speaker, I am sort of surprised to hear my hon friend speaking so disparagingly of by-elections. He was calling for one and he predicted he was going to win.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: One of the best 10 you have in Quebec.
No, let's have a general one!

Then I find my hon. friend is saying that the farmers are looking for some quick answers. I am informed by the Minister of Justice that, when the Leader of the New Democratic Party was in Regina, he was asked for his drought program and he said it would be issued during the next election campaign.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is exactly right. We had to wait a long time.
That will be a drought for the NDP.

I can't think of anything more offensive than issuing those things during election campaigns. My hon. friend, if he has anything to say on behalf of the farmers, should say them now. Canadian farmers, east and west, have found in this Government a ready friend and trusting ally. We have responded with alacrity before and we will again. Right now the farmers are hurting and this Government will help them.

Mr. Speaker, I say to the Prime Minister that the Minister of Justice is wrong again. If he had attended the press conference, he would have heard that we called on the federal Government to produce the $80 to $100 per head
June 27, 1988

of cattle. We also called for an emergency program of the kind the Government promised in 1985 and still has not delivered.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE ANNOUNCEMENT OF ASSISTANCE
REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE ANNOUNCEMENT OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Since the need is pressing now on the Prairies and since the Government could find $163 million to spend in a by-election, will it announce the $100 million that is badly needed by the farmers on the Prairies today instead of waiting for an election when the Government can find money to spend?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE ANNOUNCEMENT OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is more and more disturbing to see the socialist leader reproach the federal Government for spending money in Quebec or elsewhere, whether during an election campaign or not. That fact is, as he very well knows, that the Canadian Government in no way spent $163 million in Lac-Saint-Jean- he knows that very well. It is a falsehood that he is no doubt repeating inadvertently.
Regarding farmers in western Canada, Quebec and throughout the country, they know very well that unlike the previous Government, we never told farmers that they could go sell their own wheat.

We never said: "Go sell your own wheat". We said we were going to help the farmers of Canada and that is what we have done consistently since we have been here.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF KENYAN MINISTER OF ENERGY

subsubtopic: REPLACEMENT OF 727 AIRCRAFT FLEET-CRASH OF AIRBUS A-
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if manure production is the mark of expertise in farming, the Prime Minister takes the hat hands down.

subsubtopic: REPLACEMENT OF 727 AIRCRAFT FLEET-CRASH OF AIRBUS A-
speechtext:
Look whose talking!
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: REPLACEMENT OF 727 AIRCRAFT FLEET-CRASH OF AIRBUS A-
speechtext:
My question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. It concerns Air Canada's announced planned replacement of its fleet of 727s. The reported leading candidate for replacement of the 727s is the Airbus A-320. The Deputy Prime Minister will know that yesterday in France, during a demonstration flight, an Airbus 320 crashed resulting in three deaths and nearly 100 injuries. Indeed, I am sure all Members regret the loss of life and the injuries. The cause of that crash is yet unknown.
Can the Deputy Prime Minister assure the House that Air Canada will not proceed with what is reported to be a $3 billion purchase of new aircraft until a full and complete investigation is undertaken to ensure the air worthiness and safety integrity of the Airbus 320 aircraft?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry St. Germain (Minister of State (Transport)):
subsubtopic: REPLACEMENT OF 727 AIRCRAFT FLEET-CRASH OF AIRBUS A-
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the Hon. Member, we would offer as a Government our sympathy to the victims of that unfortunate incident in France.
With respect to the Member's question, I believe it is best answered by reading the press release of Air Canada. President Pierre Jeanniot has said no decision has been made on which new aircraft it will buy. The airline is also considering planes from Boeing and MacDonald Douglas. No decision has been made at this point and I believe it would be premature to pass judgment on any decision at this time.

subtopic: REQUEST DECISION BE POSTPONED PENDING INVESTIGATION OF CRASH

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subtopic: REQUEST DECISION BE POSTPONED PENDING INVESTIGATION OF CRASH
speechtext:
The
Airbus 320 is the first non-military aircraft in the world to use a fully computerized flight control system. Outside of military aircraft that kind of system is not being utilized anywhere else. Today in France the company's official spokesman indicated that the crash may have been caused by pilot error. That comment was made before any investigation whatsoever was carried out. The company has an interest in saying that.
Once again, can the Minister of State for Transport give the House the assurance that Air Canada will not consider, nor will it take any decision to buy the A-320 Airbus aircraft until such time as a complete investigation has been carried out and that investigation has been verified independently by Canadian officials to ensure that, if that aircraft flies in Canada, it is an aircraft that meets with the kind of standards we set in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry St. Germain (Minister of State (Transport)):
subtopic: REQUEST DECISION BE POSTPONED PENDING INVESTIGATION OF CRASH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, the investigation of the French civil aviation authorities is under way. I think it would be premature for anyone in this House or anywhere else to pass judgment or to make any comment with respect to this investigation because it may prejudice the investigation.
As far as the decision being made is concerned, I cite the words, I have full faith in the board and the management of Air Canada. They are still in the process of making their

June 27, 1988
Oral Questions
evaluations. They have not made a choice. We have said this in the House before and we are saying it today. I am sure all in this House would agree that a thorough evaluation should be done before a selection is made.

subsubtopic: WESTERN DROUGHT-CATTLE FEED QUERY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture. More than two million head of cattle are caught in the severe drought zone in western Canada. Farmers and ranchers have been moving old hay at considerable expense to maintain this herd. Has the Government yet decided what the crop insurance rule should be for turning cattle into the dried out crop as cattle feed before it, too, turns brown and blows away?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: WESTERN DROUGHT-CATTLE FEED QUERY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in response to an earlier question, there have already been some modifications announced by provincial officials with respect to crop insurance. I do know, and the Hon. Member will appreciate, that the recommendation he suggests is one which has already been offered by the industry and is a point of the discussions currently taking place between the federal Minister of Agriculture, the provincial Ministers, and those officials representing them. I would suspect there will be some announcement in the very near future.

subtopic: SUGGESTED USE OF PASTURE LAND IN WILDLIFE SANCTUARIES
SUGGESTED USE OF PASTURE LAND IN WILDLIFE SANCTUARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that we will eventually hear an announcement on this matter. For several weeks people have been waiting. Some crops have now gone beyond the pasture stage and have been completely lost to those cattle.
Is it the Government's intention to make any use of the close to 40,000 acres, or 15,600 hectares, of pastureland in the wildlife sanctuaries, including the Last Mountain Bird Sanctuary in my riding, since the birds do not eat the grass and will not be using it in July and August anyway? It would be a nice reciprocal arrangement in this time of stress since they were eating and have always eaten farmers' crops in the surrounding areas in years past.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: SUGGESTED USE OF PASTURE LAND IN WILDLIFE SANCTUARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do know that with respect to the Hon. Member's last point certainly one of the ongoing conflicts between the farming community and the supporters
of the wildlife community is the type of conflict of which he speaks.
Having said that, I know that officials are trying to find all available resources for feed which can be used in the shortterm. As the Hon. Member knows, a number of cattle have been moved off the range to northern areas. Some have been brought into Manitoba. In addition to that-

subtopic: SUGGESTED USE OF PASTURE LAND IN WILDLIFE SANCTUARIES
speechtext: No thanks to you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: SUGGESTED USE OF PASTURE LAND IN WILDLIFE SANCTUARIES
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Regina West says: "No thanks to you". One of the things that farmers in western Canada know is that when the drought took place in 1984-85 we were there with assistance to cattle producers with respect to so much per head. They also have faith in our record. They know that because we were there in the past we will be there in the future. They believe in us. Quite frankly, they are very grateful. One of the things for which they can be grateful is the fact that we are the Government of the day rather than the Party of the Hon. Member.

subtopic: SUGGESTED USE OF PASTURE LAND IN WILDLIFE SANCTUARIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: NORMALIZATION OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS WITH U.S.S.R.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs and concerns our relations with the Government of the Soviet Union. The diplomatic saga is taking on very worrying and regrettable proportions and I would like to ask the Secretary of State whether he intends to take measures to restore normal relations with the Soviet Union as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: NORMALIZATION OF DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS WITH U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member and the House know that the Soviet Union was involved in activities here which were unacceptable to Canada. I addressed those in a statement in the House the other day.
This afternoon I will be meeting the Ambassador of the Soviet Union to Canada. I have called him into my office.
The Hon. Member will also know that I have been in touch with him, representatives of the New Democratic Party, and with the Chairman of the Standing Committee of the House, with respect to a confidential briefing this afternoon on some of the circumstances which have led Canada to take this action.
June 27, 1988

subsubtopic: STATUS OF INTERNAL SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 22, the Minister told this House:
We are confident that Canadian security was not compromised and that
Canadian authorities have acted to preserve our security.
Can the Minister still maintain this position and confirm for us that this statement made last week still stands today?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATUS OF INTERNAL SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND RAILWAY DISBANDMENT-COMPENSATION FOR WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister stated in this House last Monday that the railway workers of the Newfoundland Railway supported the financial package which closed the Newfoundland Railway and would provide $70 million for labour adjustment. Was it because they had been deceived by the statements of the Minister for International Trade and the President of CN into thinking that the $70 million was available for negotiated benefits over and above what their collective agreement or employment contracts required?
Will the Deputy Prime Minister end the uncertainty among workers and confirm, first, that there is no extra $70 million available to the employees in addition to the contractual obligation of CN; and, second, that this money is not part of the Government's contribution since CN is already obliged to make these payments to its workers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry St. Germain (Minister of State (Transport)):
subsubtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND RAILWAY DISBANDMENT-COMPENSATION FOR WORKERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe the Hon. Member knows that the negotiations will take place on July 5. I think anything that we do at this point in time could possibly damage any negotiations that will take place. The package that will be put in place will be one of the most generous that this country has ever seen.

Mr. Speaker, the confusion that the Government has created among the workers of CN in Newfoundland is astounding. The workers were convinced that the Government has a package of $70 million over and above their contractual obligations. I now hear that this is not the case. Why does the Minister not come clean and tell the people the truth?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry St. Germain (Minister of State (Transport)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I repeat again that it would be premature and irresponsible to make any statements until we have sat down and properly negotiated the agreements as laid out.

subsubtopic: DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS FEDERAL LANDS IN METROPOLITAN TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for the Treasury Board. It involves the disposal of federal surplus lands. When the federal Government is disposing of surplus lands it has a policy of offering them first to provincial Governments, and then to municipal Governments, before making them available for housing.
Will the Minister direct the Bureau of Real Property Management of the Treasury Board to adopt a housing first policy so that when surplus lands are disposed of, particularly in areas where there is a housing crisis such as Metropolitan Toronto, they will be offered first for badly needed housing before anything else?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subsubtopic: DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS FEDERAL LANDS IN METROPOLITAN TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House should know that since we took office in 1984 we have adopted a policy of reviewing the federal Government's landholdings and wherever possible disposing of excess federal property. To date we have sold some 492 properties. That has returned to the Treasury some $171 million.
Specifically with respect to the Hon. Member's question, I would tell my hon. friend that a review of federal landholdings in the Toronto area is presently under way. Once that is completed it is a question of discussing the matter with the provincial and municipal authorities and deciding on the best use of that property. That decision will be taken at that time.

June 27, 1988

emergency situation cannot make do with a tape recorder that answers "This is a recording".

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women

In other very sensitive situations like this, I know that he has taken a very active role behind the scenes in a way that has been helpful to the parties. That will continue in this case. I am sure when he returns he will be able to respond directly.

subsubtopic: POSTAL SERVICES REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister responsible for the Post Office. For some time Canadians have been protesting the Government's destructive post office policy which has meant the closure of rural post offices, and the denial of door-to-door service in suburban areas in an arbitrary fashion.
Does the Minister believe that Canadians will accept, as a substitute for a change in policy, the appointment of a paper tiger that has no decision-making power, headed by a known Tory who makes donations to his political Party?
Does the Minister not realize that Canadians will see through this effort to escape the political heat on the eve of an election?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: POSTAL SERVICES REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the rhetoric in the Hon. Member's question is evidence in itself why it would be useful to have an independent third party evaluate questions as to changes in service policies, rates, and so on.
For example, the Hon. Member talks about concerns regarding changes in rural post office delivery mechanisms, yet in his own province independent polls indicate that those affected by the changes find them quite proper and over 85 per cent approve the changes. It is far preferable to have an independent third party look at those questions than to have the type of rhetoric put forward by the Hon. Member as some basis for making decisions.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister. If this Committee is going to be as objective as those polls were then Canadians are in for a mean surprise.
If the Minister wanted this committee to be independent and wanted the Post Office to operate independently, why did the Minister not give it decision-making authority? Why did he choose to appoint a known Tory to head this committee, if he wanted it to be seen as an independent body?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the board will have five members. The appointments were made today of Mr. Alan Marchment, who did an excellent job of studying the Post Office and task force report, and who is clearly one of the Canadians most knowledgeable about the operation of the Post Office; Mrs. Sally Hall, past President of the Consumers' Association of Canada; and Mr. Claude Senneville, a former member of the National Energy Board. speechtext:

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
When the House rose at 1 p.m. the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East had the floor.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, when this debate was adjourned for lunch, I was saying that it was wrong for the Government to cut funds for employment and training when unemployment was still a serious problem and felt to be a serious problem in Canada. To support my position, I referred to the report published last week by the advisory council to the Minister of Employment and Immigration with respect to older workers.
As Hon. Members know, we do not have much opportunity during Question Period to respond to the answers of the Minister. We have two questions and she has two answers, and she gets the last answer. She said that the unemployment rate for older workers went down. Obviously she has not read the report.
It is true that the official unemployment figure went down, but the Minister did not say that 41 per cent of older workers between the ages of 55 and 64 who had lost their jobs in the last number of years had withdrawn from the labour force
Supply
because they had given up hope. Consequently, they are not counted in the unemployment figures. If the Minister would take the time to read the report which was published last week on June 22 entitled Unemployed Older Worker Phenomena: A Problem That Will Not Go Away, she might be stirred to action.
In my remarks this morning, I pointed out that the unemployment figure of 7.8 per cent is misleading and does not tell the whole story because the great improvement in the employment situation has occurred in southern Ontario. There are still five provinces with serious unemployment rates. In addition, we have the problem of older workers. I also referred to the report just published on Thursday in Quebec pointing out that one out of three unemployed persons in Quebec is a young person between the ages of 14 and 25. Once again, we have a serious employment problem that deserves more investment and funding, not less.
All of this goes toward explaining the Gallup poll results published last week indicating that 27 per cent of Canadians believe that unemployment is the biggest single problem in Canada. That figure of 27 per cent leads the percentage for all the other problems identified in the survey. One would think that the Government would take serious note of these Gallup polls.
If everything is going as well as the Government says it is, why does 27 per cent of the population indicate that unemployment is still the most serious problem? These people are saying that it is the most serious problem because the improvement has other been regional and there is still serious unemployment in the regions. They are saying that it is serious because it is a very drastic problem among older workers.
I have here the report on older workers entitled Older Workers: An Imminent Crisis in the Labour Market. The advisory council to the Minister is calling this an imminent crisis in the labour market. That is why we get Gallup poll results like the results to which I referred. We also get those results because of the report published in Quebec dealing with young people in that province referred to in this morning's Le Devoir.
There are other serious underlying problems with respect to employment that are hidden by the national figures published from month to month. One such problem is the growing trend toward part-time and temporary work. This type of work has been increasing since about 1979 or 1980. The previous Government appointed the Wallace Royal Commission to study this phenomenon and to come up with recommendations, which it did, but the recommendations have not yet been implemented by the Government. Wallace and her commission recommended that unemployment and other benefits be prorated for part-time workers because of this growing phenomenon.

June 27, 1988
Supply
It is these kinds of things which are providing insecurity to Canadian workers in the labour market. Even if Canadians workers have jobs they are fearful of what will happen tomorrow because they are working usually in part-time or temporary work. Now, as opposed to the past, these jobs are at minimum wages, are low paying, non-union, and without benefits.
As you well know, Mr. Speaker, during the recession of 1982-83 many full-time industrial jobs were eliminated and were replaced by a high percentage of service jobs which on the whole, do not provide the wages, the benefits, and the security provided by the former industrial jobs. This is a serious problem to be addressed by the Government, and the Government is not addressing it. With the unemployment rate alone at 7.8 per cent, it is really nothing in which to take great comfort. Certainly, as a national figure, it is an improvement over the rate we had in the depth of the recession in 1982-83, when we registered the highest rate of unemployment in January, 1983. In the year prior to the recession, in 1981, the rate of unemployment nationally was 7.5 per cent in Canada. It jumped to 11 per cent in 1982 and to 11.9 per cent in 1983; then unemployment started to decline after January, 1983. This Government takes a laissez-faire approach to the problem and believes that if it withdraws from the market and from its spending and intervention into the economy everything will turn out well. Of course it is turning out well in the Golden Horseshoe surrounding Toronto and in southern Ontario generally, but that approach is not helping the Atlantic provinces, B.C., Quebec, or pockets in the other provinces where there is still very high unemployment.
I should point out that in the period 1965 to 1980, a period of 15 years under a Liberal Government, the average rate of unemployment was 5.6 per cent. That is what the Government should be comparing itself with, not with the figures in the depth of the 1982-83 recession. If the Government had a policy and the political will, that rate of 7.8 per cent would be lower than it is. This morning the Minister of State for the Treasury Board stood in the House and boasted that the Government had cut spending on government programs. As I said then, we have to examine which programs have been cut and which ones have not been cut. We note that the Government has promised to spend over $10 billion on nuclear submarines, whereas it has cut by 32 per cent the programs for employment and training while still over one million Canadians are unemployed.
In 1984 we were spending $2.2 billion on employment and training programs. This year we are spending $1.5 billion which is a cut of 32 per cent. That is not an acceptable situation when we still have the problems to which I referred- high unemployment rates in five provinces, high unemployment rates and getting worse for older workers, high unemployment rates for our youth, and the growing trend to parttime and temporary work which is low paid, non-unionized, and without benefits. No wonder we get Gallup poll results
which indicate that Canadians still feel that unemployment is the biggest problem in the country.
It is not good enough for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney), the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), whenever we ask a question about this serious problem, to stand and continually repeat the global figures that apply to the whole country. Of course Ontario has a 4.5 rate of unemployment. Good for Ontario, Mr. Speaker. There is a Liberal Government in Ontario which is willing to intervene and do something. The rate is good in Ontario and in a few western provinces, but the policies of the Government to lower the rate of unemployment right across the nation are inadequate. The advisory council to the Minister, appointed by the Minister and her predecessors, is saying very frankly that what is being done is not enough.
The Government's neo-Conservative, laissez-faire economic policies are misguided and are not working. The rate of fulltime job creation is inadequate. It is overwhelmingly centred in southern Ontario and it has bypassed youth and older workers; nor is there any political will to deal effectively with part-time work, regional development, functional illiteracy, labour market adjustment, and the transfer from school to work by young people.
I urge the Government to increase its spending on training, employment, and education rather than to cut those budgets. Let the Government start by cutting the program for nuclear submarines and putting the money into something that will benefit all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was most interested in the comments of the Hon. Member urging us to put more instead of less money into the government Estimates. I note that over the last few months there has been a number of suggestions by the Liberal Party for the Government to spend more money. For instance, at one stage the Liberal Party called for an increase in the budget for Indian Affairs and Northern Development. At another stage the Liberal Party called for more money to be spent on multiculturalism. Then another Liberal Member of Parliament called for $3 billion to be spent on child care spaces. In addition, I understand that the Liberal Party, if it is ever re-elected, will institute home delivery for everyone. As well, today we heard the Liberals suggesting very substantial farm subsidies. We know the Liberals want an increase in foreign aid spending, and they have called for more people to be eligible for spouses' allowances. They also want the unemployment insurance system to provide more benefits. They have suggested subsidization for prices paid to oil producers. Those are only a few of the suggestions for increases in spending made by the Liberal Party in the last few months.
Could the Hon. Member tell us how much all that will likely cost the Canadian taxpayers and from where will the money come?
June 27, 1988

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is correct that we have suggested there be additional spending in many areas, areas which we believe would stimulate the economy because it is expenditure on investment rather than expenditure on matters which will do nothing to help the economy. It will be very difficult for us as Liberals to match the side-show put on two weeks ago when the Government decided to spend $163 million in one constituency simply to win one by-election. That has been worked out to, I think, around $6,000 per elector in Lac-Saint-Jean. When the Government wants to win a byelection it starts spending money like crazy without any attention to what the outcome of the expenditure will be.
Let me say that there are areas where we must spend more money. We must do it in order to bring about social justice, and we must spend more money to stimulate the economy. The area I was talking about, training and education, is as much an investment in infrastructure of this country as investment in airports, ports, roads, and economic infrastructure. A trained work force is essential for a modern economy. To cut money in training our work force and putting people to work is complete nonsense. It is the kind of thing one cannot stop and start easily. Once it is stopped it is very difficult then to start it up and hope to bear the fruit of that start-up in a short period of time.
We all know that it takes five to six years to train an engineer after university. It takes a long time to train archaeologists, metallurgists, and so on. Trained personnel are not trained overnight. Once you cut programs for these people and they become unemployed, or there is no opportunity for young people and middle-aged people to go into these fields of work, you are left without skilled workers and professionals for a period of time. I see, in Toronto, in the area from which the Hon. Member comes, there is now a shortage of skilled workers. Of course, what happens is, we have a shortage of skilled workers in Toronto and a high rate of unemployed unskilled workers in Atlantic Canada and elsewhere.
I would submit, Mr. Speaker, not enough attention has been paid to training, employment and education in this country by this Government.

speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Guelph.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to be able to participate in this debate today on the Estimates for the fiscal year 1988-89. In the time available to me, Sir, I would like to discuss one portion of the Estimates, mainly transfer payments. In doing so, perhaps I might indicate to the House and to members of the general public just how much money we do transfer to individuals, to other provinces, to organizations, during the course of the year.
The federal Government is involved very deeply in the whole question of transfers and in particular say to individuals. But if we look at the Main Estimates for this year, we will find that $57 billion, nearly half of the total federal Government budget, $57 billion, is included for transfer payments. Also, grants to individuals, groups, associations, other levels of government, but unlike the operating and the capital expenditures, these grants that are made to these organizations or individuals are not made in exchange for any good or any service. They are outright transfer payments.
Generally, the transfer of payments can be grouped into broad categories. Individuals, subsidies, payments made to organizations and groups and, finally, the payments made to other levels of government.

June 27, 1988
Supply
The dynamic, as we now know, the dynamic economy of this country, certainly for the last four years, is recognized as a challenge to this Government in particular. We must sustain it and we must be prepared to respond to the positive thinking of Canadians. Effective social policies will continue to be needed. If we look at the spending in the area of transfers to persons, to individuals, it represents over $22 billion. Twenty-two billion dollars, or 40 per cent of all the transfer payments made, are made to individuals.
I don't have the time here this afternoon to go through all of those transfer payments. I would like to pick out just a few and give some numbers. I don't think most Canadians realize just how much is involved. Canadian seniors, if we look at them, Sir, what a marvellous group they are. They need and deserve our support. Payments made to the elderly in the form of Old Age Security benefits, Spousal Allowances, Guaranteed Income Supplements, those alone will exceed $15 billion this current year. That is an increase of over $900 million over the previous year.
Mr. Speaker, that tells me that you have a Government sensitive to the needs of the people growing a little older, sensitive to the social needs of our time. An increase of $900 million in one year alone, that is over 7 per cent, Sir.
Let me break those down. Old Age Security payments, as you know, they are made to all eligible Canadians who are over 65 years of age. They will exceed $11 billion in the year in which we are talking. This is some 8 per cent more than last year. More people coming into the group and, of course, the amount going up, in terms of the CPI. The total Guaranteed Income Supplement, which many Canadians regretfully must be on, will amount to almost $4 billion this current year.
Spousal Allowances. As you know, we took a dramatic action in terms of Spousal Allowances early in our mandate. They are forecast at $525 million in the current year. You remember, as I said earlier, we extended that down to 60 years of age, so people between the ages of 60 and 64 could take advantage of that significant program.
Now, I think all Members of this House know that this Government is dedicated to defend and strengthen the institution of the Canadian family. The Main Estimates for 1988-89, include $2.6 billion in Family Allowance payments, to families with dependent children. Beginning in 1986, you will remember that the Child Tax Credit was increased and it will reach a level of $524 for each child in 1988, an increase of $140 a year since we restructured that particular tax section. Further, beginning in 1989, the Child Tax Credit will be indexed to increases in the CPI, in excess of 3 percentage points. Another one, obviously, and somewhat dear to my heart, is what we have done for veterans. The contributions and sacrifices made by Canadian veterans have long been held in deep respect by all Canadians. The Government continues to provide benefits, some $1.2 billion, to this group through Veterans' pensions, training and education assistance to the children of those who gave their lives for our protection, in
World Wars I and II. This assistance is provided always through the Department of Veterans Affairs. It covers the cost of the Aging Veterans' Program, health care services not provided by the provincial schemes, and one of the ones that have been, in my estimate, Sir, the most significant. The veterans in the Home Program, improvement to the home program, which I know hundreds of veterans in my riding have taken advantage of.
There are other examples of transfers. Some examples of agricultural subsidies include those grants to producers which are under the Special Canadian Grains Program, freight assistance on western feed grains for livestock, assistance for the storage costs of grain, premiums on livestock, and subsidies on milk and other agricultural commodities. Payments to producers for named agricultural commodities under the Agricultural Stabilization Act will be in the order of $300 million for 1988-89.
We have demonstrated over and over again our commitment to producers and farmers, particularly in the West, through an additional contribution in 1988-89 of $289 million to the Special Canadian Grains Program. That is the balance of the $1.1 billion assistance package for 1987. In addition, as you know, we contributed over $1 billion in 1986 to help overcome the subsidy problem. The total support to grain producers for 1986 and 1987 under the Special Canadian Grains Program amounted to over $2 billion.
I could include as well, Sir, the $663 million for subsidies to railway companies under the Western Grain Transportation Act for this fiscal year alone. This reflects again the positive outlook of the Government in terms of helping those in difficulty and generating the Canadian economy across the country.
We make transfer payments of another $10 billion to various organizations and groups of people under a wide variety of programs including, for example, our Official Development Assistance Program to developing countries. Canada need not take a back seat in terms of our ODA or external aid. We contribute 0.5 per cent of our Gross National Product each year and not many countries do better than that. We continue to support the International Monetary Fund, and the Government is now embarked on a major change in how we develop our Official Development Assistance Program as a result of what Canadians told us when we travelled the country.
On another matter, we must recognize that almost $2 billion will be paid to organizations, corporations, groups, communities, employers, and businessmen to help improve the employability of Canadians through training and work experience programs, which programs are designed to take people from one job to another, to update people, to move them into the age of current technology, even to help people who, in many cases,
June 27, 1988

do not know how to work. They have never had the opportunity to work and have to be told how to do it and what is required of them. We must teach them the discipline of the workplace.
I do not have the time today to go into all the details, but no review of the federal Government's expenditure plan, and in particular the broad category of expenditures called transfers, would be complete without some mention at least of the transfers to other levels of government. In 1988-89, cash transfers to the provinces, territories, and municipalities will amount to nearly $23 billion. This represents roughly 40 per cent of the total transfer payments or nearly 20 per cent of total budgetary Main Estimates. This does not include tax sharing with the provinces to give them tax room. The federal Government has backed off in certain areas so that the provinces can take them over. I think that is what all federal Governments must do in order to be fair in terms of tax distribution across the country.
Payments to other levels of government will, as in the past, continue to be channelled through a wide variety of transfer programs. There are unconditional programs, or general purpose transfers; general support arrangements, such as those in health and post-secondary education; and a variety of specific purpose transfers.
It is not my intention to deliver a history lesson to Members of Parliament, many of whom, I am sure, have more experience in this than I. I would, however, like to spend a few moments describing the mechanisms that have been implemented over the years to promote the other two aspects of intergovernmental fiscal relations and indicate how this Government has furthered their development.
With regard to fiscal harmonization, the measures that have been put in place, such as the tax collection agreements, the reciprocal taxation agreements, and the grants in lieu of municipal or local taxes-and I may say that in some instances that represents a lot of money to municipalities-are all intended to permit the federal and provincial Governments to exercise fully their respective taxing powers in such a way as to foster fiscal harmonization and eliminate needless complexity in the income tax system. It is always going to be complex, but the very fact that the federal, provincial, and municipal Governments have been able to share some of these responsibilities has made it much simpler than it might have been.
Over the years the federal Government has recognized the provinces' demands for greater flexibility and autonomy in pursuing the achievement of certain social and economic objectives. We have agreed to various changes which have been requested such as tax credits and tax rebates. However, in permitting these changes the federal Government has had to be selective in order to ensure the progressivity of the combined federal and provincial tax systems, to maintain the administrative benefits which accrue from an integrated tax system, and to avoid compromising the operation of the Canadian economic union by the erecting of fiscal barriers to
Supply
the normal flow of capital. We must recognize that the provinces have their rights as well. I think all federal Governments have tried to be very sensitive to that.
I spoke earlier about the Municipal Grants Act under which the federal Government will transfer funding to certain municipalities in lieu of the collection of taxes on federal property. That is of some significance in my riding and I know that it is of very great significance in the ridings of some Members where there is a preponderance of federal government land and buildings. Consider the situation right here in Ottawa if the federal Government did not follow through on its promise under the Municipal Grants Act.
It is true that much of Ontario has been very prosperous and that some other provinces are doing very well. However, that prosperity does not extend across the whole of the country. The equalization program is meant to overcome that regrettable situation. It has been a major source of revenue for certain provincial Governments. Transfers under the Canada Assistance Plan and Equalization Payment Fund represent 40 per cent or more of total provincial revenues of the Atlantic provinces, one third of the total provincial revenues of Quebec and Manitoba. In the past, EPF and CAP payments represented between 20 per cent and 25 per cent of the provincial revenues of Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, and about 15 per cent in Alberta.
It would be a mistake for someone to believe that all is well in Ontario and that it receives no funding at all from the federal Government. Ontario is a great recipient of EPF alone for health care and post-secondary education. Probably 50 per cent or more of the post-secondary system in Ontario is funded by the federal government transfers.
The most important component of current federal-provincial arrangements for lower income provinces, with which we should be concerned today, is the fiscal equalization program which has been referred to as the cornerstone of Confederation because it shares across the country. It was introduced as a distinct program in 1957 and has continued to receive the support of all Parties in this Parliament since that time. We recently extended it for a further five-year period.
The Constitution of 1982 states that the purpose of these payments is to ensure that provincial Governments have sufficient revenues to provide reasonably comparable levels of public service at reasonably comparable rates of taxation. That is an important point in terms of our Confederation.
Payments under this program raise the per capita revenue generating capacity of the lower income provinces to a prescribed level which is currently the average per capita revenue generating capacity of the Provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia.
There are absolutely no conditions applied to these funds. Provinces are free to use them as they wish, to raise their level

June 27, 1988
Supply
of public service, lower the level of taxation, or undertake some combination of both. The largest transfers are those arrangements made through Established Programs Financing. That is the program I mentioned earlier and about which I grew to know a great deal in my career. Under these arrangements, the federal Government, via a combination of cash and tax transfers, contributes on an equal per capita basis to the financing of provincial and territorial insured health services, extended health care services and post-secondary education. The total cash and tax transfers under the EPF arrangements is expected to be $18.5 billion in 1988-89. That is a 5.3 per cent increase over last year. The provinces may do what they wish within that general bound.
In conclusion, the Government has repeatedly stated its commitment to the objective of national reconciliation, social justice, economic renewal and constructive internationalism. These Estimates that were tabled by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) show a reaffirmation of those objectives and a reaffirmation of what this Government has and will continue to stand for.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have news for the Hon. Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard) about the deeds of the Government he supports that will most likely dampen his unwarranted enthusiasm.
I will put it in the context of the environment, particularly the environment in Toronto where the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke to an international scientific conference. The Prime Minister attempted to portray the Government of Canada as a great protector and defender of the environment.
In these very Estimates before us in the House today for debate, the facts and figures reveal the real face of the Government, which has mercilessly cut the Department of the Environment since it took office in 1984. Let me give the facts that will remove the facade the Prime Minister attempted to erect this morning.
First, let us look at the over-all picture. Since September, 1984, when the Government took office, the Department of the Environment has steadily and systematically lost to inflation. Its estimates have not managed to keep at par with inflation while other Departments have managed to do better than inflation. The net result of this erosion caused by inflation has been a loss of $71 million in revenue to Environment Canada just to keep at par with where it was. The Member for Guelph and the Member for York East (Mr. Redway), who is very keen on the environment, will be interested in those figures.
What does that mean in terms of people? The net result is that over 300 person-years have been lost to the Department. When we raise this matter in committee, the Minister defends his position by saying that while his Department is not doing well with inflation, other Departments are developing environmental policies across the board. While this may sound good in theory, the fact is that these Departments have been carrying out these functions for virtually the last 10 years. Whether it is
the Department of Agriculture, CIDA, Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Energy, Mines and Resources, Fisheries and Oceans, National Health and Welfare, Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the National Research Council, the Science Council or the Department of Transport, those functions are nothing new. There is nothing new going on here in terms of environmental programs and mandates that other Departments have.
Who is the Minister trying to fool with that kind of explanation? The fact is that when one starts to analyse the situation, one finds that, in addition to loss to inflation in the range of $71 million and 336 person-years over the last four years, there is cancellation of programs. For example, there is the cancellation of the Guelph-Toronto Toxic Chemical Research Centre in the very city from which the Hon. Member for Guelph comes. That was an $8 million project. We find a cut of $3.8 million, resulting in a loss of 72 person-years, in the Canadian Wildlife Service. We find the termination of the Water Resources Research Grants Program. There is the elimination of research of renewable energy sources at the National Research Council. This is at a time when we are becoming more and more conscious of the fact that in the long term nonrenewable sources of energy will be running out and we must develop the know-how and technology needed to replace gradually non-renewable sources of energy. But the Government cuts research in that field. That is a shame.
Research on PCBs was eliminated. Research on toxic chemicals at the National Research Council was eliminated as well. On top of that, as you know, Mr. Speaker, there was the closure of the Marine Ecology Laboratory in Nova Scotia in recent months.
If Members would like a detailed analysis of what happens this year in the Estimates before us for debate and scrutiny, I will take Members through them step by step. Referring to the 1988-89 Estimates of Environment Canada, first, we find that the Department of the Environment this year has lost 1 per cent to inflation. It has lost 78 persons. The breakdown is rather revealing. In conservation and protection, we find in the field of inland water activities, Environment Canada this year is losing 14 persons. In the field of conservation of wildlife, budget cuts mean the elimination of five officials. In the field of management and common support, which is a general term to describe technical people, support people and office staff, no fewer than 36 people will be lost this year. So much for conservation and protection.
Let us move to the weather services. Here we find a reduction in weather services of 32 person-years this year. Last year there were 1,925 people employed across Canada. This year there will be 1,893, a loss of 32 persons. In addition to that, in the climate services, which is an emerging issue-we hear and read in the media about the greenhouse effect, the changes in climate in the years ahead-one person is eliminated. To make it even more ironic, this year the Government will
June 27, 1988

close the weather stations in Vancouver harbour and in Sachs harbour. That is not all.
We can look at Parks Canada which plays an important role for a variety of reasons. Canadians enjoy our parks. There is a recreational and cultural component there. There is also a number of jobs that depend on the activities of Parks Canada. Nine individuals will be out this year in the Resource Protection Branch of Parks Canada. In the very necessary activity of providing information and interpretation services to visitors, the Government is laying off 21 individuals from Parks Canada. When it comes to parks maintenance, we find in the Estimates a lay-off of 25 individuals. With respect to research and planning and policy development, which is very important in a Crown agency of that size, we find a lay-off of seven persons. That is not the end of it.
We used to have a Wildlife Toxicology Fund. This fund was meant to carry out research in wildlife that would give us signals and information as to what is happening inside the bodies of wildlife species with respect to accumulation of toxic chemicals and traces of toxic substances so we know what is happening in the food chain. It is a very important alert system for human beings. It is highly regrettable to discover that this fund was reduced from $1 million a year to one-third of a million dollars in the Estimates of 1988-89.
In addition, there will be the termination of the Sewage Treatment Facility Construction Program. Last year there was still left something like $2 million. This year we find nothing. I see present here a former Mayor of York East who is, I am sure, extremely receptive to this kind of problem. He has demonstrated that in committee on a number of occasions in a very progressive and helpful manner.
The Government of Canada, at a time when everyone is increasingly preoccupied about the quality of our water, at a time when the Science Council of Canada produces a report called the Year 2020 and the condition of our waters at this time, we find in 1988 the elimination of such a program. The municipalities every year at the convention of a Federation of Canadian Municipalities repeatedly asked for a federal participation. My Party is committed to provide the federal share in an amount that runs into the billions of dollars.
We find the cancellation of the Sewage Treatment Facility Construction Program, but the Government is capable and has the political will to find the necessary money to build nuclear submarines. For that project the priority is valid, but for the protection of our waters, the political will has disappeared. There is nothing left. This is the first year in my recollection that the fund available for the construction of sewers is zero. That is quite an indictment. It is a sham and a real disgrace.
The last item in the review of Environment Canada's budget for this year is in its development budget. Parks Canada has lost almost $4 million. In other words, it has lost the funds that are required to maintain and expand its network. It is interesting to compare the performance of Environment Canada, the issue which the Prime Minister invoked as being a high
Supply
priority in Toronto only a few hours ago, in terms of its Estimates with that of other Departments. What do you find? You will find, Mr. Speaker, that in this fiscal year the budget of Environment Canada goes up 3.6 per cent, which is roughly one percentage point below the rate of inflation.
How does the over-all Government increase in performance run this year? We find that the spending of the Government of Canada increases by 8 per cent in this fiscal year. Yet if we start to examine Department by Department we find some pretty startling information.
For instance, we find that the budget of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources goes up 30 per cent, while that of the Department of Agriculture goes up 24 per cent. We find that the budget of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans increases by 23 per cent while the budget of the Department of Finance manages to command an increase of 13.5 per cent. We find that the budget of the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs goes up 11.5 per cent, while the Department of Communications budget goes up 11 per cent. We see that the budget of the Department of National Defence increases by 8.3 per cent, while the budget of the Department of Transport increases 7.3 per cent.
Yet what does Environment Canada get in this fiscal year? It gets 3.6 per cent. At the same time we have in Toronto the Prime Minister of Canada making grandiose speeches about his Government's priorities for the environment, a grandiose mask that he puts on. Contrast that with the reality of the figures that are embedded in the Estimates where the facts are to be found. What a sham. What a Government we have.
It is a Government of public relations, of claims that are not supported by facts. It preaches one way and acts another. It is simply disgusting. That is all I can say to you, Mr. Speaker.
It is the same Government that in 1985 decided to impose a 6 per cent tax on insulation materials and equipment that go with the maintenance and construction of renewable energy machinery. It is the same Government which in the Budget this year had not one item that directly or indirectly related to the protection of the environment or incentives that would give encouragement to the development of an environmental industry in Canada. There was not one word on accelerated write-offs on pollution abatement equipment to create new industries and new jobs for which competitors, such as Japan, are extremely active these days.
Japan knows that there is an emerging market in this area. It knows that there is a potential for new jobs and for markets abroad. Yet there was not one word in the Government's Budget despite the great claims of the Prime Minister in Toronto this morning. There was nothing in the Budget of this year on energy efficiency-not one word on energy conservation. Yet we know that Japan, for instance, is a very clever and capable energy efficient nation. It is capable of producing at

June 27, 1988
Supply
lower costs its products because it knows how to use to its maximum the limited energy that it is dependent upon.
There was nothing in the Budget, something which I said before and something which I will not belabour unduly, with respect to helping municipalities modernize and build sewers and water treatment plants.
One conclusion is only fair and justified in relation to these Estimates and to the Budget this year. It is that they make a mockery of the claim of the Minister of Environment, which he made in 1986 in this House when he said: "We continue as a Government to be totally committed to protecting the environment". It makes a mockery of that sentence. It puts the Prime Minister in a most embarrassing position for saying one thing in Toronto in the presence of an international audience, claiming that the Government gives environment a high priority on its agenda, compared to the reality of the Estimates and the reality of the Budget of this year.
I would like to say a few words if time permits about trade because under the Estimates we have to deal as well with current issues. Trade is a very important matter that has an impact on the environment despite claims to the contrary made in the House by the Minister of the Environment.
It is very revealing to notice that if there has been one Department that is silent on the question of trade, a Department which has not produced a brochure claiming the miracles that the trade deal would achieve for Canada, it is the Department of the Environment. That is very revealing. There is not only that to consider but the fact that at Estimates time officials of the Department have confirmed that no internal study has been conducted as to what the impacts of the trade deal would be and how they would impact upon the environment. I am referring in particular to the question of pesticides which is included in the trade deal and the requirement in that section that American and Canadian regulations be harmonized.
What does harmonize mean? No one knows. What will be the repercussions of harmonizing American with Canadian regulations? No one knows because no one has studied them.
In Question Period there have been a number of questions in your presence, Mr. Speaker, on various occasions in which we have asked from this side of the House why beer is excluded from the trade deal. Not a word has been mentioned about water. Why has lumber been referred to in the trade deal as being exempted but there has not been a word about water? Why was processed fish mentioned as an item to be exempted by the deal and not water?
We cannot get an answer to those questions. Yet we find it very strange that the Government would go to great lengths to identify and itemize three items in our economy to be exempted but has not mentioned water which is such an important natural resource to us.
Time does not permit me to go into greater depths in a debate such as this on the implication of the trade deal on the
environment. I thank you for the opportunity to speak, Mr. Speaker, as well as for your patience.
Mir. Redway: Mr. Speaker, I have had a good deal to do with the Hon. Member in the past four years. I have come to feel that he is a most sincere Member of Parliament, particularly in his dealings with the environment. I know of his commitment to the environment. However, as he went through the Estimates of the Department of the Environment for this year I had the sense that he equated wholly and solely the question of an effective federal environmental policy with the question of how much money is being spent on it.
One of the items I noticed, for instance, was that he talked about the fact that the weather service was going to be reduced by one person. In May of this year I had occasion to travel to the Northwest Territories and to visit Resolute Bay, among other places. We have a weather station at Resolute Bay. I had an opportunity to see that weather station. It was pointed out to me that a very sophisticated computerized piece of machinery had been installed recently at that weather station which would give us a great deal more information about the weather than we had ever had before. It would give us a great deal more information about the ozone layer over the Arctic than we have ever had before. In fact, it had already disclosed important new facts about the ozone layer in the Arctic. The strange and interesting part is that all of this was going to be accomplished with the elimination of one person from the weather service. I do not think the Hon. Member's conclusion follows that, by throwing more money at a thing and by having more people on staff, automatically there will be a better Department of the Environment, by any manner of means.
The Hon. Member is most sincere in his comments. I know that he is really expressing a frustration with the Liberal Government of which he used to be a member. As the Minister of State for the Treasury Board (Mr. Lewis) said earlier in the debate during the five years that preceded the Government taking office, when the Hon. Member was a member of the former administration, government spending went up an average of 15 per cent a year across the board. In spite of that, as the Hon. Member is aware, there was no program developed with targets for reducing acid rain emissions, as there has been with this Government. There was no program with targets for reducing nitrogen oxide emissions, as there has been with this Government. There was no agreement between Canada, the United States, the State of New York, and the Province of Ontario with respect to reducing the amount of toxic chemicals going into the Niagara River and the Great Lakes, as there has been with this Government. There was no national park on Ellesmere Island under the previous Government, in spite of that 15 per cent increase in spending each year, but there is under this Government. There was no national park on the Bruce Peninsula, but there has been under the Government. In addition to all of that, there was not a Canadian Environmental Protection Act under the former Government of which the
June 27, 1988

Hon. Member was Minister of the Environment, but there has been under this Government.
I would like to put it to the Hon. Member, does he not really wish that he would be, should be, and could be a member of this Government, a Government with a truly effective environmental policy?
