speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) is a good politician, but a poor psychologist. In interpreting people's frustrations he should do better. I am sure he could do better if he were to try a bit harder.
The point that he made on the sophistication of computerized equipment in weather reporting is quite accurate. The statistics of the Estimates this year that I put on record refer to a cut of 32 people in the weather service and one person in the climate service for a total of 33, which is a considerable cut that cannot only be attributed to sophisticated computerized equipment. In addition to that, in Vancouver the closing of a weather station is a development which is rejected very strenuously by the fishermen's union because they have had a number of instances where even the most sophisticated equipment could not forecast a sudden change in weather as a human being does by way of binocular observation. Therefore, that is a very serious matter from the point of view of preventing the loss of life.
In analysing the performance of the previous Government- the Hon. Member was not in Parliament at that time, otherwise he would know-one finds that in March, 1984, the Liberal Government launched two initiatives, a federal-provincial one in which all seven provinces including the Province of Ontario, which was represented by the Party to which he belongs, agreed to a reduction program of sulphur dioxide. That commitment in March, 1984, was renewed in June, 1984, when the economic and financial distribution of responsibilities was tackled.
In the same period Canada also launched an international initiative on sulphur dioxide, which led to some 21 nations getting together and agreeing that we should have a protocol, which was subsequently signed in Helsinki in 1985. In regard to sulphur dioxide, it is on record as being a good day's work before the Government of the Hon. Member came to power.
On NIX I cannot say the same. That summer we launched the concept of having a public consultations force first under the auspices of Transport Canada on car and truck emissions. Those consultations were conducted and completed in December, 1985, and then carried out by way of regulations which came into effect under the present Government. I am glad and readily recognize that evolution, but the Hon. Member for York East should not make the mistake of thinking that the world began in September, 1984. It would be historically naive, and he is too sophisticated a man to be naive. I know him well enough and I respect him for that.
On the creation of parks, we are happy that Ellesmere was created. It is in addition to the 21 or 22 national parks that
Supply
were created in preceding decades by successive Liberal and Conservative Governments. I do not think that national parks is the monopoly of any Party. We all believe in that policy. We are glad to see Ellesmere added. In addition, both Ellesmere and Bruce Peninsula came pretty close to being announced before September, 1984, but things being complicated in life, one does not always get his or her way when he or she wishes things would happen.
Nevertheless, I do appreciate the question from the Hon. Member. I can assure him that I am very happy where I am.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity this afternoon to say a few words in connection with the matter before the House, which is officially referred to as an Act for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the Government of Canada for the financial year ending March 31, 1989. That is a large mouthful. In simple terms it boils down to something that we know in this House and the federal Government talks about as the main spending Estimates for 1988-89.
To the average Canadian it is not a question of spending Estimates, it is something that they know in their own terms as their Budget. Every Canadian has a formal or informal budget by which he or she spends his or her money. By and large Canadians know where their money is coming from, how much they will earn in a year, and how much they have available to spend. Therefore, they set their spending priorities in terms of their own budgetary arrangements in order to spend a certain amount and hopefully save a certain amount of that total income.
One of the things that differs between the average, ordinary Canadian and Government is that the ordinary Canadian cannot spend more than is coming in, whereas Government always seems to have that facility. In fact, on a regular basis it seems to spend more than it earns, or that it takes in through the tax system whether it be income taxes, customs or excise taxes, or federal sales taxes. The Canadian public knows one cannot spend more than is taken in, unless one borrows some money to pick up the difference. That is what has been happening for a substantial number of years. That is why we have the enormous accumulated deficit that we have, and that is why we have an ongoing series of annual spending deficits. Fortunately, however, in the last four years, those have been getting progressively less, and now we are under $30 billion a year, but $30 billion a year is still a heck of a lot of money and it is still a great problem for the Government and for all Canadians when trying to get a handle on the finances of Canada.
I have always tried to follow the principle in public life, whether municipal or federal, that Canadians as a whole want to see the Government looking after their money and spending their money as effectively and as efficiently as possible and keeping the waste down to an absolute bare minimum, if not

June 27, 1988
Supply
eliminating it altogether. That is a principle with which all of us would agree. When we look at the spending Estimates or, in layman's terms, the Budget for 1988-89, that is the sort of thing that I feel and that I believe the Canadian public feels we should always keep in mind. If we are going to collect money in taxes and then spend it, how can we keep those expenditures to an absolute minimum and still do an effective job? How can we make sure that not a dollar of it is wasted?
This year, the proposed Main Estimates total something that, to the average Canadian, would boggle the mind. It totals something in the vicinity of $119 billion. That amount is broken down into a portion which is called statutory spending. That means that we have already passed laws saying that no matter what else happens, we will have to spend that money each and every year unless we repeal those laws. Then there is a portion called discretionary spending, and in that portion, we do have some leeway as to whether we spend more, less or the same amount in a given year.
Statutory spending is the kind of spending that most of us would not quarrel with whatsoever. It is spending on things like social transfer payments. I see the Hon. Stanley Knowles sitting at the Table. He knows how hard he fought for old age security, for unemployment insurance and for family allowances. All of these things are part of what we know as statutory expenditures, and part of the statutory authority for those expenditures involves indexation according to the Consumer Price Index or according to inflation.
Each year, regardless of what sort of deficit we are running and what kind of money we are bringing in, we have to continue to spend money in accordance with statutory requirements, and each year we have to spend more money because the statutes providing those funds provide for indexing in each and every year. That portion of the annual expenditures, the annual Estimates or the annual Budget of the Government, continue to rise as long as the Consumer Price Index continues to rise, and no one seems to have been able to do very much about that for a long time, probably since the 1930s, and none of us would want to go back to that time. It is inevitable that that portion of our expenditures will keep going up each year, whether we like it or not.
The second part has to do with discretionary expenditures. When we talk about discretionary expenditures, someone always suggests that we reduce some of them. We hear our colleagues in the Liberal Party and the NDP saying, "Oh, no, you can't reduce that expenditure, you should actually be spending more money on it rather than less". Whatever it is that we try to reduce, tighten up or spend more effectively and efficiently on, someone in either the Liberal Party or the NDP will say: "No, no, don't cut that, cut something else. We don't know what you should cut but don't cut that. In fact, you should be spending more money on that".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext: They only want to cut defence spending.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
That's right. They do not want to do that either, though. Although members of the NDP say that we should not be spending money on nuclear-powered submarines, they do say that they themselves would spend at least that amount if not more on conventional weapons and another kind of defence system. They are not suggesting that anything should be cut; they are suggesting that there should be more expenditures.
How do we go about trying to ensure that the money we spend as a Government and as a Parliament is spent as efficiently and as effectively as possible? I could spend a long time on that, but I would like to touch on just two things. The first has to do with taking a close look at the way Government operates and seeing if there is not another way of doing it better. In that respect, I would like to single out one example of how Government can do something better, and in fact, how Government has been doing something better in the last four years.
I am talking about the question of cash management, the management of the cash the Government takes in and the matter of how it expends that cash. That is something that has been commented on before by the Auditor General. In his 1984 report, he had a good deal to say about the way we were managing our cash flow in Government and about the savings that could be effected if we did it differently.
The Public Accounts Committee, of which I am a member and of which I was a member in 1985, examined officials of the Treasury Board, the Finance Department and the Department of National Revenue. Through our questioning, we were able to identify and get commitments from these officials about things they would do to try to improve the cash management of the Government. In fact, as reported in the press in 1985, we got out of them that in the next year, the 1986-87 fiscal year, they would commit themselves to savings of something like $40 million through better cash management.
It is interesting to note that in March of this year, the President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) made an announcement on the steps that had been taken in cash management. Even better than the commitment made back in 1985, the President of the Treasury Board indicated that a progress report on cash management in the Government of Canada showed estimated savings by the end of the last fiscal year of some $220 million, and there was a forecast of further savings of $120 million for the current year, the year for which we are now debating the Estimates, and another $419 million in cash pulled back into the Consolidated Revenue Fund from Crown corporations.
It was estimated at that time that the total savings from improved cash management in the Government would reach the figure of $1.2 billion. That is a very substantial savings in revenue. It is a savings that has been accomplished by doing things better, not by doing things the same old way. This has shown that we can spend the people's money more efficiently and more effectively and not waste as much as we have been
June 27, 1988

wasting. It shows that we can do things better, save some money and help cut back on the deficit without savaging the other spending Estimates that concern the Opposition so much.
How has this been accomplished? A number of things have been brought to bear. A number of new policies have been instituted, and I would like to touch on just a few of them. The first of these has to do with the way the Government pays its bills. In the past, as soon as the bill arrived, the Government issued a cheque. Even if the bill provided 30 days to pay for it, right away the cheque went out and the bill was paid. In fact, by using a process that all business utilizes, namely, paying bills due in 30 days in 30 days so that you do not have to pay an interest penalty but you are then not putting out money ahead of time, losing interest that you would get on it if it were sitting in your own bank account, by making payments on time rather than ahead of time it is estimated that the Government will save approximately $50 million each year.
Second, there is the whole question of making payments to Crown corporations, which need some extra infusion of cash because they are not taking in enough money to pay for all the things on which they spent. In order to save some money, to do things better and to manage our cash more effectively it was suggested that, instead of handing Crown corporations a lump sum payment once a year, perhaps we should make periodic payments to them when needed and not just hand money over to them when we get the bill which says we are supposed to pay them some money. The Government has been following that procedure in the last three years or so. As a result, instead of Crown corporations having a surplus of cash in their bank accounts while the Government was borrowing money to cover its immediate expenditures, money has been sitting in the Government's bank account. In the meantime, it is earning some interest. That has amounted to a saving of more than $400 million.
Other practices have been instituted as far as money management is concerned. One is the use of travellers' cheques and travellers' credit cards, a standard business and personal practice on the part of most Canadians, something which the Government had not been doing in the regular course of events. That is significant because each year the Government spends something in excess of $500 million on travel expenses for its employees. Any particular savings in that area obviously will be significant.
Another area is modern banking methods, the use of direct deposit of cheques and the electronic transfer of funds. This is something which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was Leader of the Opposition spoke about prior to the last election. He spoke about the way in which money could be saved. The Government is now starting to institute this sort of policy and there is more coming down the pipe very shortly of which I am personally aware. Again, there is more money to be saved by doing it better through better money management.
Supply
Another method is to ask people to pay the money owed to the Government. Instead of being slack and letting things slide we are now starting to ask for the money when it is due and getting it in. That has amounted to a savings of approximately $100 million over the last three years by asking people to pay their bills.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has amended the requirements with respect to withholding taxes by large corporations. Instead of the payments being made monthly they are required to be made twice monthly. That has had a one-time revenue impact of $1.2 billion for the Government of Canada. You can see that in all of these ways the Government has acted during the last three years on the advice of the Public Accounts Committee, the Auditor General, the initiatives of the President of the Treasury Board and other Ministers, and it has come up with some very substantial savings and ways of doing things better. That is the sort of thing in my view that I am looking for as a Canadian taxpayer. I am sure all other Canadians are looking for that as well.
I would like to comment on another way that we can do things better to make sure taxpayers' money is not wasted and is spent as effectively and efficiently as possible. It has to do with the way we treat the estimate or budget process as far as Government is concerned. The estimate or the budget process as you know, Mr. Speaker and as I know, is really at the root of the British parliamentary system. This is a process whereby, theoretically at least, you and I and the other Members of Parliament sitting here are supposed to control the expenditures of government. The Government is supposed to come to us cap in hand and say, "We need money to spend this year. Will you please grant us the spending authority?" That is not the way it works in practice. The Government puts together its spending Estimates. Hopefully, the Government is very careful in the way it is put together, and the Minister of State for the Treasury Board (Mr. Lewis) indicated in his comments that that has been the case in the last four years because the average increase in expenditures in the last four years, as I understand it, has been only 3.7 per cent, less than inflation, whereas with the previous Government, for the five previous years the average increase was 15 per cent.
The Treasury Board and the Government have been careful, and I commend them for that. But we should be looking at a better way of doing things as far as Parliament and Members of Parliament are concerned. We should be looking at a process whereby there is a true estimates-budget committee which examines in detail the budgets of each Department and has the authority and the right to reduce spending expenditures and budget items so that Canadians can feel that Parliament is there to protect and to look after their dollars to make sure money is being spent effectively and not wasted. The only way we can really do that is if the Government will concede that its spending Estimates are not absolutely and essentially a matter of confidence in the Government. There is no reason why Parliament as a whole cannot act to reduce the Government's spending Estimates on any particular item or

June 27, 1988
Supply
across the board or why the Government should have to feel that it is a vote of non-confidence in the Government. For heavens' sake, the next day or the same day a motion can be put before the House saying, "Does this House have confidence in the Government?" I am sure that 99.99999 per cent of the time the House would pass that motion of confidence notwithstanding the fact that it felt the Government could have been cut back on its expenditures in one or two items.
That is why the Public Accounts Committee, in its twelfth report to Parliament, recommended that sort of process. That is why the Public Accounts Committee approved the other day a special study on improving parliamentary control of the budgetary process. That is why I hope that in the fall we will have a new type of budgetary process with an estimates committee which can actually reduce government expenditures without causing the Government to fall. That would be a very significant step forward in assuring the people of this country that they have a Parliament which will make sure and do everything in its power to see that their hard earned tax dollars are spent as efficiently and effectively as possible and are not wasted.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the speech made by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway). Would he care to comment on the following situation, of which I am sure he is aware being a diligent Member of Parliament? He will know that in the City of Toronto in his own riding the unemployment rate, the last time I looked, was 3.9 per cent. It hovers between 3.5 per cent and 4.2 per cent. In some parts of Newfoundland the unemployment rate is around 28 per cent in some large regions, according to officials of Statistics Canada. The Member will also know, having listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) last August talk about the OECD report on Canada's performance and growth, that part of the report said that in Canada in the last year the economic disparity between the regions was noteworthy for its starkness. The Member will also know that the Economic Council of Canada in October said that uneven regional growth in Canada is the most serious economic problem facing the country.
In view of those facts, of which I am sure the Hon. Member is well aware as are you, Mr. Speaker, would he care to comment on the fairness to the Atlantic region of Canada which contains one-tenth of all Canadians? Would he care to comment on the fairness of this Government putting into the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, an agency supposedly designed to assist Atlantic Canada to overcome the economic disparity, putting into that part of the budget 15 per cent of 1 per cent, a very, very miniscule commitment from this Government to a problem that has been identified as the most serious economic problem in Canada? To say that we will spend an additional $200 million, 15 per cent of 1 per cent of the national budget of Canada, surely does not sound like a commitment by this Government to overcome this problem.
I know the Hon. Member is from Toronto, and I know the people of Toronto are doing very well financially in this country, in terms of unemployment rates and whatnot, but the people of Atlantic Canada are still suffering. I am afraid this Government has not seen fit to do anything about it. I would like to ask for his comments on that. I am sure he is sympathetic to that, even though he is from a part of the country that is doing very well.
Mr. Red way: I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his comment, his question. I am pleased that he has drawn attention to the fact that, according to OECD figures, which represent figures for the industrialized nations of the western world, over the last four years Canada has had the best rate of job creation of any country in the industrialized western world. Over those years, Canada has had the best rate of economic growth, generally, of any of the countries in the industrialized western world.
The Hon. Member pointed out the fact that in the Metropolitan Toronto area, in particular, the employment situation has been extremely good, and there is no question about that. In fact, the latest figures that I have show that the unemployment rate is in fact less than what the Hon. Member referred to. I believe they are presently at the rate of 3.2 per cent, and traditionally, economists have considered 3 per cent as full employment.
So, it is quite clear that in the Metropolitan Toronto area, there is full employment even in the traditional sense of the economists of the Second World War era, that now, the economic situation in Metropolitan Toronto is excellent, indeed. That can be seen regularly by the fact that there are signs in virtually every business window, help wanted signs, asking people to come in because they desperately need help.
I am aware that there is a very substantial rate of unemployment in the Province of Newfoundland, but I am also aware that that has fallen as well over the last four years. The most recent figures, and unfortunately I don't have up-to-date ones-but the most recent figures I have in front of me are from December, 1984, to January, 1988. In that period of time there was a drop in the unemployment rate in the Province of Newfoundland by 6.4 per cent, over the rate in September of 1984, when this Government took office.
Now, I realize that people in Newfoundland do not necessarily want to come to Toronto to work, even though there are jobs in Toronto. That is understandable. I certainly would not want to contribute to the depopulation of Newfoundland by suggesting that all Newfoundlanders, or a good portion of them, should come to Toronto to seek employment.
We do have a very interesting problem now in this country, where we have an actual shortage of help in a good many areas in the Metropolitan Toronto area, while we have a surplus of people who are unemployed in other areas of the country.
June 27, 1988

The employers in Metropolitan Toronto would dearly love the people from Newfoundland to come to join them and to obtain work there. Alternatively to that, the employers in Metropolitan Toronto say to me, "If the people of Newfoundland and other parts of the country, where there is unemployment, do not want to come to Toronto, we need workers. We understand that they would not want to come. We understand that they do not want to depopulate their own communities and their own provinces, but if they do not want to do that, we do need workers. We do need them desperately. Please allow an increase in immigration from other countries so that people will come to Toronto and fill these jobs that are desperately needed".
I agree with the Hon. Member, that there is still a problem, in spite of the fact that progress has been made, not only in Toronto and in Newfoundland and all across the country, as the Hon. Member knows, but there is a very substantial improvement. In fact, we have in the country today, I think everyone would have to agree, the greatest prosperity that Canada has ever experienced, although that does not say that it couldn't be better and that there are not other parts of the country where we wouldn't like to see it better.
I wonder if the Hon. Member would be prepared, in return for further commitments of effort and assistance on the part of the people in central Canada, in Metropolitan Toronto, to support a policy of increased immigration to this country so that we could actually get more people to do the jobs that are there waiting to be done in the Metropolitan Toronto area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I found that exchange a very interesting one. It is no wonder that the people of Newfoundland, the Maritimes and the West look with such aggrieved eyes upon the City of Toronto. The Hon. Member just suggested that if the people from Newfoundland, and presumably the rest of the country, do not want to move to Toronto, and presumably in large numbers constitute a portion of the food lines and victims of a housing shortage there, then we should fill the need in Toronto by inviting more immigrants. No one more than I favours increased immigration to Canada, under the proper circumstances, in which we have the kind of economic growth that would allow that immigration not only to occur but to lead to the prosperity of Canada.
First of all we should take cognizance of the fact that, in all probability, those invited to Toronto from Newfoundland or elsewhere to Fill the job vacancy needs, would likely not have the kind of training they ought to have in order to fill those jobs, and that would be because of the decrease in expenditures for training that this Government has forced upon the country since it came into office.
My hon. colleague on the Liberal benches indicated earlier that they have cut, since coming to office, programs for
Supply
training from $2.2 billion to $1.5 billion. It seems to me that it is impertinent and arrogant for Toronto to say, "We are doing great, come on down, and if you don't want to come down and leave your home, then come on, let's have somebody take your place in Toronto". I think that is just unacceptable. But, Mr. Speaker, that would be consistent with the attitude of this Government and is related indeed to some of the questions that I had hoped to have had an opportunity to explore in my intervention this afternoon.
In thinking about this debate, I became aware of some speculations about the purposes of free trade. You will recall that at the time that this Government came to office, there was a great deal of optimism in the big business sector of this country that this was a Government that at last would give the cutting of the deficit a high priority, cut the number of civil servants, cut down on social programs, and in general use as victims the poor, the elderly, and others, in order to enhance the profitability of major industry and major investors.
You will recall, however, that among the initiatives was the cut-back on pensions through deindexation. I am sure you will remember the confrontation between a little old lady and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) before these very doors. She convinced the Prime Minister that it would lead to a rather severe political punishment if the Government proceeded with the approach of enhancing the comfort of big business in Canada at the expense of ordinary Canadians who have perceived this land for a very long time as being socially just. For all three Parties, until this Party came to office, social justice had a very high priority and it was not tampered with in the interests of the relatively few rich. This lesson learned by the Prime Minister was kind of disappointing but gave the Prime Minister an opportunity to think in other terms.
Someone has suggested a scenario during the meeting between the Prime Minister and the President of the United States. The Prime Minister was expressing a great deal of regret that he was unable to pursue this kind of approach to cutting social expenditures, and the President of the United States said, "Well, Brian, if you were more like us you would not have problems with people protesting when your Government attempts to cut back on social programs".
He suggested an approach which would permit the Government to fulfil the requests of its large contributors, the big business people and big corporations which have wanted cutbacks in government expenditures and lay-offs of civil servants and so on. He said that one of the first things to do was to start privatizing and start deregulating. He said that in order to deal with the question of social expenditures, unemployment insurance, medicare, pensions and all the rest, he was going to have to become more like the United States, and that the only way to become more like the United States was to become commercially part of the United States. He said that if the Government did that, business decisions would be made in the American competitive context in which there is no medicare,

June 27, 1988
Supply
no unemployment insurance, no proper workers' compensation program, and no family allowance. He said that the pressure which would be exerted by the threat of American companies saying that they would bring their subsidiaries home and so on would ensure that we cave in, but that it would be business pressure and the inevitable consequence of the competitive, market-driven environment which will be established when free trade is established.
The President of the United States said, "By God, Brian, you won't have to stand up as the Prime Minister and as a government and say that this is being done, it will inevitably be done". The Prime Minister said that that was a good idea, that up until now he has been against free trade but if that is the only way he can cut social expenditures without suffering the political consequences, then maybe this is what we should do.
My hon. colleague says that that is not what the Prime Minister described as the reasons for entering into the free trade agreement. He said that the free trade agreement would allow Canadian businesses to have a larger market. To those of us who said that that is not what this is all about, that it is about all that Canada is about, he said that those who oppose this do not believe that Canadians can compete, that we are the Chicken Littles who think the sky will fall in if we are faced with competitiveness with the United States.
We had to look at this seriously. Did the Prime Minister really think that Canada would be in a position to survive in a competitive environment? Let us look at what has been transpiring in this country as a consequence of government action or inaction and see whether there is any realistic opportunity for us to compete.
One of the clear elements of competitiveness in international trade is research and development, the availability of a highly educated workforce and a well trained workforce. If we are going to compete with a country like the United States we had better have the capacity to innovate, to create new products, and to enhance our manufacturing.
The question which must then be posed is whether Canada is now or is likely in the immediate future to be in a position to compete effectively and whether the Government is doing the things necessary for that competition. In other words, the question is whether the Government really believes that the country is in a position now, or will be in the short term, to compete with the United States or any of the other OECD countries on the basis of what exists or those initiatives which have been taken.
Let us look at our situation. It has been repeated over and over again in this House that Canada's rate of expenditure for research and development is only one half of that of the other OECD countries. Canada spends only 1.34 per cent of its GNP on research as compared to about 2.5 per cent spent by other countries. We rank twelfth in the rate of research expenditure among the OECD countries.
Japan has 240 scientists and engineers per 100,000 population, the United States has 260 per 100,000, and we have 90. With regard to the percentage of research investment in this country done by industry as compared to the other players, Canada's research effort is funded by industry only to the extent of around 50 per cent as compared to as much as 70 per cent in, for example, Switzerland.
This is a ridiculous situation which obtains in our country which is symtomatic of our failure to have made the investments in research and development which we ought to have. It is ridiculous that 80 per cent of the equipment used for resource extraction in this country is imported. Eighty per cent of the equipment required for getting our oil, coal, and minerals out of the ground is imported.
I am sure my hon. colleague from St. John's East understands that if we were really being competitive those big business people, mainly foreign-controlled, would have invested in manufacturing capacity. In fact, this country suffers a $7 billion technology deficit in trade. This figure has doubled in the last 10 years. The whole thing deteriorates.
When we look at government promises to increase the commitment to research and development, what do we find? Since the present Government has come to office, research and development expenditures have actually decreased. They have decreased as a percentage of government expenditures in every year since the Government has been in power, this in spite of the fact that the Prime Minister has made innumerable promises to make Canada a leader in research and development. He has failed utterly. Granted, there has been a lot of symbolism and a lot of rhetoric.
We must congratulate the Hon. Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) who has done a journeyman's job of trying to sell the notion that research and development ought to be increased in this country. However, he has failed utterly with the Prime Minister. For example, the Prime Minister promised in January that an additional $1.3 billion would go into research and development and that of that some $200 million would go to the granting councils.
One of the interesting things which the Prime Minister did was to form an advisory committee on research. A member of that committee wrote a report which said that over the next two years there ought to be a doubling of the investment in the granting councils and that thereafter there ought to be a rate of increase of 1.5 per cent, the rate of increase in the Gross Domestic Product. Instead, $200 million has been spread over five years. That results in a 2.7 per cent increase for NSERC. There has been a significant increase in the commitment to the expenditure on the space station. It was supposed to cost $800 million. There was a great deal of concern expressed that this would distort expenditures in other areas of research and development which the country just as desperately needs.
June 27, 1988

Now we discover that it will not be $800 million, but $1.2 billion. A great part of the increased expenditure will come from the $1.3 billion in additional money in research and development that the Prime Minister promised. We learn further that there are likely to be increasing demands for increased expenditures for that space station.
The Government has set aside $240 million of that $1.3 billion for centres of excellence. A great deal of those expenditures will be concentrated in Ontario and Quebec which, as the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) has already recognized, have benefited to a great extent already.
Our comparative position with the rest of the world with respect to research has not significantly improved as a result of government action. I have cited the $1.3 billion promised by the Prime Minister, spread over five years. When the Government first came to office it cut expenditures in the Departments of Fisheries and Oceans, Environment, and Agriculture. It ravaged the National Research Council. Much of the increased expenditures being touted now really are a compensation for cuts made in the past.
The core of the issue is that there has been no net increase in the position of this country with respect to its competitiveness in research and development and consequently its general competitiveness, since the Government came to office. Free trade is supposed to be a great boost to our competitiveness. We understand that competitiveness is founded on capacity for innovation which, in turn, is dependent upon research and development. Everyone recognizes that as a consequence of free trade there will be a good deal more dominance in our economy by American owned companies.
One must recognize that one of the reasons for our pitiful performance in research and development has been that many of our industries owned by American and other foreign investors do very little research. Compared to Canadian-owned companies, American-owned companies spend about half for research. The rate of investment in research and development by Canadian-owned companies is about 9 per cent or 10 per cent of sales. However, the rate of investment in research and development by American-owned companies in Canada is about 4 per cent to 5 per cent of sales. The deficiency in the amount of investment in research and development by industry in this country is largely because our industries are dominated by foreign, particularly American-owned industries that have no reason to do research in Canada.
It is of particular interest to note the example of the Auto Pact. Although the Auto Pact has provided assurance of a certain level of employment and production in the automobile sector in Canada, one result has been the repatriation of all engineering design and research to the United States. My City of Windsor, which had a significant engineering and managerial capacity, no longer has it because of the tendency for the parent plants to concentrate research and development and management in the United States.
Supply
In spite of the fact that the Prime Minister said we were minor league with respect to research and development, little has been accomplished in this area in the last four years, whether it be in universities or industry.
This contrasts with a very vigorous and concentrated program to enhance research and development in all the countries against which we must compete. Of course, there is the question of universities themselves. I am sure the House is familiar with reports emanating from all across the country, most recently from Ontario, which indicate that our universities are in a sorry state. The Government has failed to ensure that the provinces have an adequate level of transfer payments. It has also failed to come to grips with the necessity that the provinces must pay their share. It is another example of tragic neglect.
If one looks at what has happened in the United States as compared to Canada in the last several years in terms of the recognition of the need to have a solid level of investment in universities and colleges, one must fear for the fate of our country's future when we are confronted with direct competition with the United States. The United States spends 25 per cent more of its GNP on universities than we do here.
The rate of increase in the level of funding of universities in Canadian provinces since 1983 has ranged from about 5 per cent to about 10 per cent. On the other hand, there has been roughly a 50 per cent increase in the rate of expenditure in places like Alabama and California. Through the United States there have been increases in the rates of funding for post-secondary education from 10 per cent to 60 per cent. In Canada it has been much less.
Surely this indicates that the Estimates we are discussing today, and the Government policy with respect to competition, have ignored an elemental fact in any trading relationship we will have with the rest of the world, let alone the United States. It is a prescription for dependency and for failure to obtain the kind of growth from innovation we might have had if we maintained our future independence and placed the investment in research and development and education and training to make this a prosperous country in the twenty-first century.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to comment on a couple of remarks made by the Hon. Member. Unfortunately, some of his assertions are false. I know he would be the first to want to correct them.
He said that over-all spending for research and science-related activities in Canada has decreased every year since the Government assumed its mandate. That statement is false. The over-all spending in these areas is measured in accordance with the Gross Domestic Product. We have experienced a spectacular growth in the economy. This rate of growth has outclassed every industrial nation in the world. If one measures our performance in research and development spending in accordance with the GNP, the Hon. Member would agree that

June 27, 1988
Supply
spending has increased. I admit that we only made marginal gains in terms of the percentage of GNP we are spending on research and development. But we did keep pace with the growth, and it is a nominal 3.5 per cent. So there has been a 3.5 per cent real growth in the spending of R & D before we talk about the additional increases that have been made. Likewise, the Hon. Member said we have only boosted the granting council's funding from previous years by 2.7 per cent. That, too, is absolutely false. If the Hon. Member looked at the real figures he would discover that in the current five year projection, the rate of increase will be in the neighbourhood of 16 per cent.
The Hon. Member has been selective, but I do not blame him for that. It is true that the $1.3 billion has been made available as a result of the Prime Minister's announcement in January for research and development this year. There was a substantial increment last year, and I cannot predict, because I do not know what the growth of the economy will be next year, what moneys will be available to boost that effort next year. However, $1.3 billion is available this year. Of that amount, $200 million is given to the granting councils to be allocated to universities in the normal fashion. I am certain all of that money will go into basic theoretical and curiosity type research.
In addition, the Hon. Member knows we have announced a Centre of Excellence Program to which we have committed $240 million. That money also will be allocated by the funding council directly to universities. It is true that the program, of course, seeks to establish these critical linkages between government laboratories and the private sector, but any private sector participation in any of these programs will be supplemented with private sector contributions to the program. So the $240 million, I hope, will become $500 million, I do not know, but the federal Government is putting in $240 million and that money goes to universities.
In addition, the Hon. Member knows we have announced in connection with this program a scholarship program which will cost $80 million over a four year period. It will give 10,000 students over the four year period a scholarship that will encourage them to pursue these future oriented careers of which the Member spoke and in which there are critical shortages, such as engineering and the natural sciences. It will entice women to aim for those kind of future careers more than they did in the past. All in all, it is not a bad record when we compare it with what we inherited when we came on the scene.
My performance is measured against what we did before. As the Hon. Member knows, the performance of the previous Government was measured in bricks and mortar. The previous Government built buildings all over the place. I confess I am pleased we have facilities such as the Biotechnology Centre in Montreal, the Marine Dynamics Institute in St. John's, Newfoundland, and the Industrial Technology Centre in
Winnipeg. Tens of millions of dollars were spent. But that was not research, it was construction.
As well, we had a so-called SRTC Program. When it was first started it was designed to encourage the private sector to spend more money on research. It did spend a lot of money, but it spent it on innovative tax accounting instead of industrial innovation, and $2 billion was lost over a 18 month period in property flips. We stopped that program. What I have put in place is a program that truly does give the private sector the incentive to do research. In fact, next to Singapore, Canada today has the most lucrative and advanced tax regime to encourage private sector research, and the results are showing in the sense that private sector has increased by 16 per cent its effort towards the total national research effort since I came on the scene.

The Minister of State for Science and Technology is a man I admire for his efforts not only on behalf of research and science but for what little success he has achieved with this Government. But in fact it has to be measured against the target which was described by the Prime Minister. He said: "In my term, Canada will achieve 2.5 per cent of GNP in investment and research". That has not happened.
The Minister says that I fail to tell the truth when I say that the rate of government expenditures for research and development have decreased. My God, these are figures from his own Department. In 1985-86, the rate of government expenditures for research dropped by 2.5 per cent. In 1986-87, it dropped by .3 per cent.

Those figures come from the publications of the Minister's own Department. With respect to this great $200 million that is going to be given to the granting council, what the Minister did not say is that that is going to be back end loaded. NSERC will receive 2.7 per cent in the next fiscal year out of the $200 million. The Minister no doubt will say there is additional money available from matching funds in the Industrial Matching Program. That is fine, but I am talking about the $200 million. Dr. Lortie, a member of the Prime Minister's own advisory council, said the level that has been accorded by Government should be doubled not only over five years but over two years. The Prime Minister's own advisory council is saying that what Government is doing is not nearly enough. We could have all of these weasel words that, yes, we have increased over-all Canadian expenditures for research and development because our percentage of GNP rate of expenditures has been maintained, but that is no excuse. What are we going to do, double the GNP next year and have our percentage devoted to research and development and once more claim that, yes, we spent a little more?
June 27, 1988

This country is far behind every other country against which it must compete-most particularly, the United States-in research and development. All the weasel words and all the little progress that has been made is not going to meet the needs of this country if it is going to compete, particularly in a free trade environment. The fact is that the Minister knows that in a free trade environment, our chances of ever developing in terms of adequate science or research will be utterly killed because the United States Government right now spends some $70 billion a year on research and development. Almost half of that is for defence research, or it uses defence research as an excuse for expenditures. We are expected to compete against that with a Government which puts pennies here and there and still has not decided what it is going to do with the other half of the $1.3 billion the Prime Minister said we are going to make available for progress.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I begin, I cannot help but regret publicly the inclination of some within the House to equate progress and expenditure money as necessarily being synonymous because, unfortunately, as you know, Mr. Speaker, that type of comparison in itself can be very incomplete and can in fact be very misleading. Unfortunately, when one looks at Estimates, one talks entirely in terms of the dollars and cents. So there is, naturally, this inclination to think in terms of money spent as somehow demonstrating in itself a commitment or lack thereof on the part of any Government towards the objectives of those moneys being spent.
I would suggest in passing that that type of philosophy while it might be, to some degree politically popular can, in the long run, be injurious to a country. It has led to some of the excessive spending which we have seen in this country and in others in the last decade or so.
The objective before the House today is to talk about the Estimates. I am pleased to be able to do so with specific reference to the Estimates of the Department of Agriculture. In the absence of the Minister I am pleased as his Parliamentary Secretary to be able to explain and, if necessary, to defend the Estimates before the Members of the House.
Having done that, and without any excessive remarks on my part, I can say in all conscience that I believe that this Government's record and commitment to agriculture is unprecedented in the history of Canada. I readily concede that the problems which we have encountered have been very substantial. That certainly justifies the expenditures of the moneys which we are now presenting to the House.
I can also say that this is not the first time in Canadian history that we have had problems in agriculture, nor will it be the last time. While we cannot resolve those problems through the mere expenditure of money, I feel that the commitment of the Government, and the commitment which is most evident in
Supply
the work and leadership provided by the various Ministers responsible for agriculture and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), is unprecedented. The Prime Minister has met with national farm leaders on, I believe, seven different occasions.
I say to those who are directly concerned with these Estimates that I think that the number of new programs which we initiated and the support which we are providing financially and otherwise does without a doubt indicate the commitment which the Government has to agriculture, and appropriately so. Because of the problems to which I have already referred it is no surprise that our support of agriculture financially is increasing. Despite the partisan differences that sometimes surface in the House I think that that type of financial support is welcomed by all Members of the House.
Spending plans for Agriculture Canada this fiscal year total some $2.16 billion, an increase of $421 million over last year's Main Estimates of $1.74 billion. In addition, there is also provision in this year's Estimates for a net increase of 66 person years, which is a point worth stressing. I hear on occasion people speaking of cut-backs within the Department of Agriculture. Of course, the reality is that we are talking about 66 additional person-years rather than a reduction in personnel.
The largest single new item in this year's Estimates is some $296 million, the bulk of which is the last part of the $1.1 billion program which will be expended during the course of this fiscal year. In fact, if I recall correctly, about 85 per cent or 90 per cent of the final cheques are being mailed this week. The balance is being mailed next week which is, of course, good news for farmers wherever they may be located. Within this $296 million there is some provision for additional personnel to be hired to administer the Special Grains and Oilseeds Program No. 2.
In 1987-88, provision for the $1 billion program which, of course, at that time was unprecedented, was provided through the Supplementary Estimates. By the end of June a total of 208,000 grain producers will have received payments under the Special Grains and Oilseeds Program No. 2. While the average payment works out to some $4,500, statistics are often misleading. I know that the farmers in my constituency are receiving on average substantially more than that. I can also report that I have had many farmers say to me quite candidly that if it were not for this program and for the payments under the Western Grain Stabilization Program they would not be able to continue farming as they are at the moment.
The purpose of the Special Grains Program is to reduce- not to eliminate-the impact on Canadian farmers of the trade war which has been taking place between the European Economic Community and the United States. It is a trade war which in all minds is evidence of the insanity which is in the international grain trading community. While we cannot match the resources of others, we are trying to lessen the impact. In addition, and something which is probably more

Supply
important, we are trying to provide the necessary leadership which we hope will mean the end of that trade war at some point in the reasonably near future.
Within this year's current Estimates there is $26 million for payments into the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, and $5 million for payments into the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Program. These programs fall within the jurisdiction of the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer).
Elsewhere, a spending increase of just under $20 million is foreseen for various provincial agri-food agreements. These are regional development agreements which are intended to improve farm productivity, to explore export opportunities, and to help develop secondary industries. These are programs which are very important, particularly to the primary sector of agriculture which is in such difficulty. Our share of these agreements amounts to $40.3 million in 1988-89.
Another program provides $11.5 million which is needed to help tobacco producers adjust to the market realities of the 1980s. This is an industry which has undergone in many ways revolutionary changes over the last two to three years.
The alternative enterprise initiative encourages research, new crop development and market development projects in tobacco-producing areas in Ontario and Quebec. There is also a tobacco transition adjustment initiative program which provides payments to producers to help them leave the tobacco industry. This program applies also to Prince Edward Island producers, as well as to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick farmers.
Estimated statutory payments under the Agriculture Stabilization Act this year are expected to total $65 million.
The Main Estimates reflect our continuing commitment to agriculture, to the farm community and to the agri-food system through new initiatives and the maintaining of longstanding programs. It is important that I take a moment to mention some of the other initiatives which the Department of Agriculture is undertaking.
In April of this year the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds officially opened the National Grains Bureau in Winnipeg. Last year, a grains and oilseeds branch of Agriculture Canada was formed because of the very large and very special role these commodities play in Canadian agriculture. The National Grains Bureau is the policy and planning arm of the grains and oilseeds branch. Its purpose is to serve as a focal point for the federal Government to participate more effectively in and to respond to grains issues. It made sense that this National Grains Bureau should be located in Winnipeg which is in many ways the heart of the Canadian grain industry.
We have also started a new program called Grains 2000. The name says it all. This program will help us design longterm policy options for grains. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, the focus during Question Period on the appropriate need for long-term policy. I am delighted that Grains 2000 is working in that direction. I think that it is an initiative welcomed by
others in the House. The idea is to give people within the grains industry, farmers, representatives of the various grain buying companies, universities, provincial Governments, and other agencies a chance to participate with the federal Government in policy development.
Having attended a number of meetings with the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds in which he has consulted with the industry on an informal basis, I find this type of consultation to be very effective. I think the investment which we are making as a Government and as a country in this type of program, and others, will be money very well spent.
Also in effect now is a transfer of the Grain Marketing Bureau to Agriculture Canada from the Department of External Affairs. There are a number of people certainly within the farming community who think that that is a change which is certainly warranted. This results in an increase in expenditure of $3.9 million, which includes 27 person-years.
For more than a year Agriculture Canada has been developing a strategic plan to guide the research branch into the 21st century. The plan is founded on something that the Minister and I, as well as everybody else interested in agriculture, really believe in-a stronger partnership between Agriculture Canada research stations and the agricultural industry, as well as our research partners in the provinces and universities.
What the plan hopes to do is to strengthen the links between Agriculture Canada research stations and organizations in the agri-food industry to bring about more joint research ventures. What is happening is that there is more of a realization that world research should indeed be a world in which government and others participate as partners. Certainly, the federal research station which has been an integral part of our history in Canada, since 1886 if my memory serves me correctly, has made an invaluable contribution. Nevertheless, having said that, we believe quite strongly that there is a role for the universities and for the provinces. For example, the University of Manitoba has a very valuable agricultural research activity. One of my alma maters, the University of Saskatchewan, also has a distinguished record in the same area. In the future, this type of partnership will be quite fruitful. We have had joint ventures before, but this type of plan will spark more research in the agri-food industry, especially for private food processing firms.
It has been said before, but it is worth saying again that Agriculture Canada has no intention whatsoever of relinquishing its historic role as a leader in the agri-food industry, but wishes a clear definition of where others fit in. That is an appropriate request, and it is probably also an objective with which it will be comfortable. It also sees government and research as being areas where there is an opportunity for partnership, and it simply wants to know what its role and the rules will be.

In accordance with the Government's commitment to deregulation, discussions on the privatization of the record of performance programs will continue with groups from both industry and provincial Governments. Privatization of recording activities is already well under way in the swine and dairy sectors. Generally speaking, it has been well received.
Our very important five-year dairy policy, outlined in January, 1986, continues to ensure that efficient producers of milk and cream receive a fair return for their labour and investment. This fiscal year the federal commitment to that program is $227 million.
Another area where we have put a great amount of effort, and perhaps to some degree with slightly disappointing results, although we see progress, is in the area of tripartite stabilization. The progress has certainly been slower than we wished, but indeed there is progress. In recent weeks there have been a number of meetings. The federal Minister will be meeting with provincial counterparts in Toronto on the 12th of July, or the week thereof, and I hope there to be more progress at that particular time. These meetings have become even more important since meetings last March in which the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) met with his provincial counterparts. There are differences, but there is a continuing commitment to resolve those differences. We will see some progress in the not too distant future.
Every Member of the House, whether a representative of urban Canada or rural Canada, is well aware of the international crisis which exists in the grain industry and is also aware of the leadership that the Government has been attempting to provide.
In our opinion, the trade agreement negotiated with the United States is helpful both as an example to the international trading community, and also in lessening some of the trade impediments which have plagued agriculture in the last two to three years.
We also believe that our participation in the current round of multilateral trade talks is exceedingly important. It is through those types of discussion that we will find the longterm solutions that we are seeking. All too often in politics the media, and to some degree the politicians, focus on the crisis of the moment. This morning's The Globe and Mail carried a story on the drought which is so significant on the Prairies. Predictably, and borne out by what happened in the House a few hours ago, much of the thrust of Question Period focused on that drought, in part because of the publicity provided to the issue by one of Canada's leading daily newspapers.
The problems which exist in agriculture exist irrespective of whether they receive the attention of journalists, or indeed the attention of Members of the House. That is why discussions which have been taking place in the international trade community are so vital. Those ongoing discussions are absolutely essential if we are to end the war in subsidies, which means that Canadians who produce a very high quality
Supply
product have been compelled to sell the product at substantially reduced prices. That is why the GATT round is so important. Our commitment and support of GATT is of absolute importance. In many ways we see that as being the real solution that the farming community and those of us who are interested in the farm community are seeking.
Those of us who are interested in agriculture, particularly those of us from the Prairies, know that we live in a world where exports are predominant. Fifty per cent of agricultural income comes from exports. Sometimes members of the urban community look at the supply management sector and ask: "Why do we not use that as a strategy to resolve all of our problems?" I have heard people on phone-in programs suggest that we sell in Canada and build a trade wall around Canada and meet the needs of the Canadian farmer. Tragically, that would mean a loss in agricultural income of 50 per cent. It would automatically mean a reduction in personnel of 50 per cent.
Our future in agriculture lies in the development of markets. To a large degree those markets will be found outside the country. There are really only two industrialized nations in the world that do not have guaranteed access to a market of at least 100 million. We are one, and Australia is the other. That is why the trade talks are so important, and why the free trade agreement is important. It provides us with an example to the rest of the multilateral trading communities of a direction in which we can go.
The GATT talks are of the utmost importance. The meetings in Montreal which will take place, the mid-term evaluations meeting in December, will give us an indication as to where we are headed. Our future lies in that type of activity. I am proud to be part of a Government that has made this a priority.
The main Estimates do not include all the expenditures which will take place in the world of agriculture. Some of those will be included in Supplementary Estimates after program specifications are provided by the Treasury Board. We are extending the Farm Debt Review Boards until 1991, which represents a further commitment of $39 million. I wish we did not need Farm Debt Review Boards, but the reality of the matter is that we do. I have spoken to many constituents who are able to stay in farming because of that type of program and financial commitment on the part of the Government and the people of Canada.
The main Estimates also do not show an additional commitment of $270 million through 1991 to the Farm Credit Corporation. That will enable FCC to enter into arrangements reached with the Farm Debt Review Board process to give it some much needed extra flexibility. FCC has been in a very severe financial crisis. If it operated within the private sector it would have been out of business some time ago. We as a Government are attempting to provide it with the necessary financial support to give it the flexibility which it needs to address its programs.

Another program we might wish that we did not need, but which is exceedingly important, is the Canadian Rural Transition Program. It has also been extended to 1991 at a cost of $28 million. Certainly, it is very difficult to think of this program in terms of successes because it is addressing the needs of people who have to leave the farm. When some must, or some choose to, it is very important that someone be there with a helping hand. That is basically where the rural transition program fits in.
In Manitoba, as a model, there have been services provided through a research institute which is located in my own community. 1 know the people who work there. I know many people who have made use of the service. It is money well spent, and money that is necessary to help in that type of transition.
Last December the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced a $75 million National Soil Conservation Program to be carried out over the next three years. This is subject to matching funds from the provinces. All the evidence indicates that the provinces are extremely interested. Anyone who travels the Prairies these days is exceedingly conscious, perhaps even painfully conscious, of the need for soil conservation programs. In some areas the ditches are full of quality soil that is the victim of soil and wind erosion. This will be an investment in the future of the country. The Farm Fuel Tax Rebate Program often talked about in the House will save farmers approximately $440 million.
When we talk about the farm community today we talk about men and women working together. That has always been the case, but perhaps we are more conscious of it today than we have been in the past. One of the expenditures in this program which pleases me is that there will be some more money, not an awful lot, but some more money available to support Agricultural Canada's farm women's program this year. That will facilitate farm women coming together to discuss the problems that are so crucial to them. Furthermore, we hope that it will also provide them with an avenue by which they can approach the Government of Canada and be part of the consultative process.
Quite frankly, the objective of all of us and of the Government is to serve the needs of the Canadian farm community by working in co-operation with them. Too often in the past Governments have attempted to devise programs which were allegedly going to solve the problems of the people of Canada. We are attempting to work with the people of Canada in order to address the problems of the day.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CONCURRENCE IN THE MAIN ESTIMATES FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1989
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this debate because our Party will oppose the Estimates that are before us. Many of the things the Hon. Member opposite has suggested are happening in his community are certainly not happening in our communities. First and foremost, the Government is going to spend, at a minimum, $8
billion on nuclear submarines. Yet it cannot find the money to increase the Estimates for the Canadian Jobs Strategy.
The Canadian Jobs Strategy has been cut by $125 million. That $125 million could have gone toward providing programs for older workers. Three times I have heard a program announced for older workers. First, a program is announced and then a year later, the Government says that it has to negotiate with the provinces. Then when it is asked what the provinces are doing, the Government says that it is just on the verge of an agreement, so it announces again that there will be a program. Sometimes Canadians are not aware of the details of what happens here, and they keep thinking that there is a program for older workers.
I want Hon. Members to know that 1,300 employees of Firestone in Hamilton were laid off this past year. I also want Hon. Members to know that many of those workers were older workers and there is no program for them. The federal Government is using the excuse that it cannot get an agreement with the provinces. It has agreements with many of the provinces now, but until it has an agreement with all the provinces, it simply will not worry about older workers. That is a very callous attitude and it is one to which I take great exception.
I also feel very strongly about the fact that the federal Government made a promise during the last election campaign of a child care program for the children of Canada. We know that two million children do not have child care spaces. There is no money in the Estimates to increase the child care that is provided to Canadian children.
I think these Estimates are a classic example of hypocrisy on the part of the federal Government. Yet, the Government can afford to put another $20 million into propaganda for selling a trade agreement with the United States that the Government calls a free trade agreement. Yes, it is free. It freely gives our country away. The Government is willing to spend money in order to convince Canadians with their own money that they should give their country away. That certainly does not make very much sense to me.
Looking at the Estimates, I recognize that the Government wants to provide some money for transition houses. I know that a million women are being battered, and the federal Government said during the last federal election campaign that money would not be an issue when serving the needs of battered women. Unfortunately, all the Government can find now is $10 per battered woman.
The Government talks about making allowances for the needs of society today. It says that it will reach out to the people. Words are cheap and the Government has been able to use those words during election campaigns. What we are looking for in the Estimates are programs. We are looking for dollars that will implement programs to give relief to the people who are suffering. The Government is not doing anything to provide for people's needs. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and certainly we do not want to confuse the issue with reality, reality being that the Government has not only defended nuclear submarines in the House but has also said that the submarines would not be in any conflict with the environment. The Government has no expenditures in the Estimates to clean up the environment. At the same time, it has announced several times that it will spend money on nuclear submarines. It is in the process of letting the contract for those submarines in the next couple of months. It seems to me that the Government certainly has its priorities skewed, and I am very concerned about the fact that with that kind of hypocrisy that is being sold to the Canadian people, this Government does not deserve to govern. I hope we will be able to put an end to it in the not-too-distant future. It will not be too long before the Canadian people will realize that the great fear of this Government is dealing with what the Canadian people really want.
I would also suggest that we do not see spending programs for housing in the Estimates. We know that housing is job creation. We know that the needs across Canada for housing are crucial. Certainly looking at what is happening in my own community makes me recognize that. A study has shown that applications for social housing in Hamilton are up by 25 per cent over this time last year. With the Hamilton-Wentworth housing authority, there are 1,253 families on the waiting list for non-profit housing.
What can the federal Government do? Certainly Canada Mortgage and Housing could look at the situation and act on some solutions. Educational programs to improve community acceptance of social housing are very important. There has been a program like this in the City of Toronto. Certainly we could use this kind of program in Hamilton. It is something that not only creates jobs but gives people a sense of security in their own communities.
I have just been looking at Canadian Business of June, 1988, not necessarily a New Democratic publication, but certainly one that has taken a very good look at the problem with employment in Canada. This publication says that politicians focus too much on job-creation programs and not enough on policies that address the more fundamental problems in the economy, and that without such direction,

speechtext:
No, if we look at what the trade agreement does, it deals with low-paid trades and the creation of low-paid jobs. It is a fundamental erosion of our economic base.
According to a survey done in 1982 by Labour Canada's micro-electronics task force, we were investing 25 hours per worker on annual retraining programs and education as compared to 35 hours in the United States and 65 hours in Japan. We must recognize that when dealing with the long term, we have to look at skills training that is outside that provided by the companies that look at the short term. Certainly these are the kinds of recommendations that came out of the study done by the micro-electronics task force.
A positive way of spending money certainly would be to invest in labour and in what the real jobs are in society without giving our country away. That would be the proper way to put the Estimates before the House. Rather than that, the Government is setting the priorities it thinks are important, not those that are important to the Canadian people, and expecting that the Members of the House of Commons will support those Estimates. I think we would be irresponsible as Members of Parliament if we approved these Estimates. Certainly with the majority that the Government has, it can do what it likes, or so it keeps telling us, both through the procedures of the House of Commons and the spending of the money of the people of Canada.
It is really important to recognize that it is the money of the people of Canada that is being spent. Certain things are not available. I see, for instance, immigrant women in this country who cannot get language training or access to the labour market and find it very difficult to integrate within society itself. They have children in schools and have to go for interviews. They need help from the health care system but cannot get access to it because of language problems. This is not a surprise to the Government. Studies have been done. We have asked questions in the House and constantly we have been told there will be movement on those programs, yet the Estimates before us do not allow for any language training for immigrant women.
These are the kinds of things that demonstrate whether or not a country cares about its society and the people who live in it. These are the kinds of programs that say not only that we welcome immigrants into society but that we want to assist them become full participants. Because of the lack of programs people coming into the country often feel intimidated and feel they are second-class citizens because they cannot participate with their family members because of a very rigid language barrier. There is discrimination between men and women. There are language programs for men but not for immigrant women. This is not only a very serious economic
