obstacle but also a serious social obstacle hindering people from participating full time in society. It is more than discouraging; immigrant women are thus unable to be the kind of care deliverers for their families which they could be if there were adequate programs for them.
It is a disgrace to be asked to accept the kind of Estimates we are being asked to accept today. Those Estimates do not reflect the promises given by the Conservative Government during the last election. Things have not come to fruition. What have we got instead? We have a great PR program which is trying to tell Canadians what they should like whether they like it or not, trying to put them in a situation where they are threatened, whether they are threatened or not. We are supposed to be imagining some kind of great attack from over the Arctic Ocean, and therefore we are supposed to put all our resources toward saving us from that. We would be a lot better off if we were building a really constructive multilateral kind of trade policy to say that the country is important, that Canadians are competitive and can be multilateral traders, instead of having only one trading partner. But that is exactly what the Government is trying to do.
What is happening? The Government is spending money foolishly. It is cutting back on useful programs. The Canadian Jobs Strategy Program, as I have said often in the House and in committee, has taken on the proper direction, but it needs to be fine-tuned. It does not need cut-backs. That kind of investment will not only help reduce the deficit in the long term but it will also help build a stable economic base, which is much more important than spending $25 million telling Canadians they have a good agreement with the U.S. when it is a lousy one. That kind of hypocrisy is not what we stand for on this side of the House.
We look at programs that are important for people. We look at those things that will build a caring society and a society with some stability. When we look at those things we realize that the priorities in these Estimates are all wrong. This is not the kind of Canada we look toward. It is not the kind of spending we think is responsible spending of Canadians' own money. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, we will oppose these Estimates. We hope they will be the last Estimates that ever come forward to the Parliament of Canada by this Government.

Mr. Speaker, I was overwhelmed by the comments of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar). First, on a number of occasions she indicated the question of nuclear-powered submarines were in the current Estimates. Of course they are not, as you are well aware. All of her remarks with respect to that were irrelevant and out of order because they had nothing to do with the issue before us, that of the spending Estimates for 1988-89.
Second, the Hon. Member referred to the fact that the Estimates and the expenditure plan of the Government was a disgrace because it did nothing for people. As you are well aware, Mr. Speaker, the expenditure plan and the policy of the
Government over the last four years have had a significant effect on those living below the poverty line. In fact, the incidence of low income people has decreased from 17.3 per cent of the population in 1984 to 14.9 per cent, which is the latest figure for 1986. It is quite clear that the policies of the Government as reflected in the spending Estimates have been a significant helping hand to low income people about whom the Hon. Member has expressed concern.
In job creation, Canada has led the industrialized western world in those four years. Canada led in economic growth in those four years. All of the things which the Hon. Member has spoken about seem to imply that her Party, the New Democratic Party, has a different approach to things. The New Democrats would have a different industrial strategy for the whole operation.
In this House recently the member of the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), made a statement. He said that the NDP's industrial strategy:
-could well mean less growth, or a bit of a standstill in growth, in the golden triangle form Quebec to Windsor.
I put this question. Why do we want Toronto or Montreal to get any bigger? What for? Glorified anthills is what they are. Why would one want to establish another manufacturing plant in that part of the country? As far as I am concerned Toronto needs another manufacturing plant like it needs a hole in the head.
Is that the Member's policy and the policy of the NDP as set out by the Hon. NDP Member for Regina West recently in this House?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) certainly does not have the authority to make or break a policy of the New Democrats, and I think we all know that. As New Democrats we have spoken about making sure there are economic policies to reduce regional disparity.
We are very concerned about the amount of unemployment existing in the interior of British Columbia, northern Canada, Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada. The present Government should be appalled by its actions which have allowed the level of unemployment to grow as it has in those regions of the country while there is an overheated economy in southwestern Ontario. It is certainly bad economic policy.
